story: Antaeus beat every wrestler who came at him, because every time he was thrown down he got up stronger. Heracles worked out the trick, hoisted him off the ground, and held him in the air until he weakened.

who: Greek god of light, music and prophecy
why: He stood for clarity, proportion and reason.
story: Nietzsche paired Apollonian order against Dionysian ecstasy and argued great art needs both — the clear shape and the wild energy inside it. The Apollo space programme took the name of the god who drove the sun across the sky.

why: She out-wove Athena in a contest and was turned into a spider for the insult.
story: Arachne's tapestry was better than the goddess's — that was the problem. Athena tore it up and struck her, and when Arachne despaired, turned her into a creature that could weave forever. Spiders are still classed as arachnids.

who: Athens's ancient council, meeting on the Hill of Ares
why: It served as the city's highest court for the gravest crimes.
story: The Areopagus tried murder cases, and myth says its first defendant was the war god Ares himself. Milton borrowed the name in 1644 for Areopagitica, his argument against censorship — a speech to a court that no longer existed.

why: Its crew sailed to the far end of the Black Sea to fetch the Golden Fleece.
mean: An adventurer on a difficult quest
story: The Argonauts were named for their ship, not their leader — argonaut simply means Argo-sailor. Prospectors racing to California in 1849 called themselves Argonauts too, which was optimistic about the fleece.

why: He put living politicians on stage and mocked them by name in front of the whole city.
story: Aristophanes wrote a comedy attacking Socrates as a fraud who taught students to dodge debts. Twenty-four years later, at his trial, Socrates complained that the play had poisoned the jury against him long before he arrived.

why: He classified everything from tragedy to squid and set the framework for European thought for centuries.
story: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, European scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

why: The Bacchanalia were his festivals, and they got out of hand often enough to be banned.
story: The Roman Senate banned the Bacchanalia in 186 BC, calling them a conspiracy. Thousands were arrested. The festivals had grown from a small women's rite into all-night gatherings the state could neither see into nor control.

why: He joined the plot to kill Julius Caesar, who had treated him as a friend.
mean: Betraying a friend out of principle
story: Shakespeare gives the dying Caesar the line Et tu, Brute — you too, Brutus. The real Caesar probably said nothing at all. Brutus insisted he acted for the Republic, not against the man, and killed himself two years later.

who: Founder of Thebes in Greek myth
why: He sowed a dragon's teeth and armed men sprang up and killed each other until only five were left.
mean: Of a victory that ruins the victor
story: A Cadmean victory costs more than losing would have. Cadmus also, according to the Greeks, brought them the alphabet from Phoenicia — so the man behind the ruinous win is also the reason they could write about it.

why: Chief of the nine Muses, she inspired Homer and the grand heroic style.
mean: Grandly epic; also loud and brassy
story: Calliope was the eldest Muse and the mother of Orpheus. In 1855 an American inventor attached her name to a steam whistle organ so loud it could be heard for miles — the calliope that still shrieks over fairgrounds.

why: Sculptors carved columns as standing women, said to represent the women of Caryae.
mean: A sculpted female figure used as a pillar
story: Six caryatids hold up a porch of the Erechtheion in Athens. One was removed by Lord Elgin and taken to London; the Athenians said for years that the remaining five could be heard at night, crying for their missing sister.

who: Ferryman of the dead in Greek myth
why: He rowed souls across the Styx, and only for those buried with the fare.
story: The Greeks buried their dead with a coin in the mouth to pay Charon. Anyone unburied waited a hundred years on the wrong bank. Pluto's largest moon is named Charon, still ferrying alongside the underworld.

why: She carried a scroll and was invoked at the opening of historical works.
story: Clio's name comes from the Greek for 'to make famous' — the historian's actual job, as the Greeks saw it. Herodotus's nine books of history were each named after one of the nine Muses, and Clio got book one.

who: One of the three Fates in Greek myth
why: She spun the thread of each human life while her sisters measured and cut it.
story: Three sisters ran every life: Clotho spun the thread, Lachesis measured it, Atropos cut. Even Zeus could not overrule them. Engineers borrowed the name for the clothoid, the spiralling curve that eases a road into a bend.

why: He ruled the Golden Age, and the Romans identified him with Saturn.
mean: Of Saturn; belonging to a remote golden age
story: Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to stop the prophecy that one would overthrow him. His wife handed him a stone in swaddling clothes instead of the sixth. The sixth was Zeus, and the prophecy held.

why: Its secret initiation rites promised a better afterlife and were never written down.
story: For nearly two thousand years, thousands of Greeks were initiated at Eleusis — and not one of them ever recorded what happened inside. The penalty for telling was death. It remains the best-kept secret in the ancient world.

who: Paradise of the blessed dead in Greek myth
why: Heroes were sent there instead of the grey underworld, to fields of perpetual ease.
story: Elysium was the good afterlife — sunlight, meadows, no work. Paris named a boulevard after it: the Champs-Elysees, the Elysian Fields. Anyone stuck in its traffic may question the comparison.

who: The Furies of Greek myth, renamed
why: Athenians called the avenging Furies 'the Kindly Ones' out of fear of naming them directly.
story: The Furies hunted murderers without rest. Calling them the Eumenides — the Kindly Ones — was pure superstition: you did not want to attract their attention by using the real name. It is the oldest recorded nickname made out of fear.

who: Wife of Orpheus in Greek myth
why: Orpheus won her back from the dead and lost her again by glancing behind him.
mean: Of something lost at the final moment by looking back
story: One rule: do not look back until you are both out. Orpheus walked the whole way up in silence, heard nothing behind him, and turned at the last step to check. She was there, and then she was not.

why: Their language and scriptures shaped Judaism and, through it, much of Western culture.
mean: Of the Hebrew language, people or tradition
story: Hebrew stopped being an everyday spoken language for roughly seventeen centuries, surviving only in prayer and study — then was deliberately revived, and is now the first language of millions. No other language has managed that.

who: Greek goddess of witchcraft and crossroads
why: She was worshipped at night where three roads met, with offerings left in the dark.
mean: Witchlike; of the night and crossroads
story: Hecate is often shown with three faces, watching all three roads at once. Greeks left food for her at junctions on the night of the new moon, and did not look too closely at who collected it.

who: Queen whose flight to Troy began the Trojan War
why: Marlowe called hers the face that launched a thousand ships.
mean: Of a beauty that causes conflict
story: Careful with the spelling: Helenic is Helen of Troy, Hellenic is Greek in general. Both trace to Greece, but only one of them started a ten-year war by leaving with a visiting prince.

why: Lame and cast out of Olympus, he made the finest armour and machines of the gods.
story: Hephaestus was thrown off Olympus as an infant and walked with difficulty afterwards — the only Greek god with a disability. He was also the only one who actually made things, including golden servants that moved on their own.

who: Youth of Greek myth loved by Apollo
why: Killed by a discus throw, and from his blood Apollo raised a flower.
mean: Of a deep purple-blue; of thick curling hair
story: Apollo threw the discus, the wind blew it off course, and his friend died. The flower that grew where the blood fell carried the boy's name. Homer uses hyacinthine for hair, meaning dark and tightly curled.

who: Homer's epic of the Trojan War
why: It covers a few weeks of a ten-year siege and made them the model of epic conflict.
mean: Epic in the scale of its conflict
story: The Iliad is not about the whole war — it covers about seven weeks near the end, and never reaches the wooden horse. Its actual subject, announced in the first word, is the anger of one man.

who: Daughter of Agamemnon in Greek myth
why: Her father sacrificed her to obtain a favourable wind for the fleet sailing to Troy.
mean: Of one sacrificed for a larger cause
story: Agamemnon summoned his daughter to the coast on the pretext of a wedding. In some versions Artemis snatched her away at the last instant and left a deer on the altar — a rescue the Greeks invented later, when the original proved unbearable.

who: River of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld
why: Souls drank from it to erase their memories before being reborn.
story: The dead drank from Lethe so they could start again with nothing. Its opposite, Mnemosyne, ran alongside — and initiates of some mystery cults were told to refuse the first river and ask for the second.

why: Its people carved elaborate tombs into cliff faces and kept their own language and alphabet.
story: The Lycians cut house-shaped tombs high into sheer rock so the dead would be closer to the sky. Their alphabet borrowed from Greek but kept extra letters for sounds Greek did not have, and nobody could read it for two thousand years.

why: Betrayed by Jason, she took a revenge so extreme that Greek audiences were shocked by it.
story: Medea gave up her home and her family to help Jason steal the Golden Fleece. When he left her for a princess, she destroyed everything he loved and escaped in a chariot drawn by dragons. Euripides gave her the last word.

why: She is shown holding a tragic mask and wearing the raised boot of the tragic actor.
story: Melpomene started as the Muse of singing — her name means 'to celebrate with song'. She was reassigned to tragedy later. The two masks hanging outside theatres are hers and her sister Thalia's, comedy and tragedy together.

why: She was the mother of all nine Muses, making memory the parent of every art.
story: The Greeks made memory the mother of the arts, which is exactly right for a culture that recited Homer from memory for centuries before writing it down. Mnemonic — a memory trick — comes from the same root.

why: She punished those who grew too proud or too fortunate.
story: Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

who: Titan of the great river encircling the world
why: The Greeks pictured a single vast stream running round the edge of the earth.
story: For the earliest Greeks the Ocean was not water everywhere — it was one enormous river running in a circle around the rim of a flat world, and Oceanus was the Titan who was that river.

why: Games were held there every four years, and the interval itself became the unit of time.
mean: A four-year period; the Olympic Games
story: An Olympiad is properly the four-year gap, not the festival — the Greeks dated events by counting them. The ancient games ran for roughly twelve centuries before a Roman emperor shut them down as a pagan rite.

why: He beheaded the Gorgon, rescued Andromeda, and was placed in the sky as a constellation.
story: Perseus borrowed winged sandals, a cap of invisibility and a mirrored shield, which is a lot of equipment for one monster. The Perseid meteor shower every August appears to come from his constellation.

why: After a brutal wrong she was turned into a nightingale, whose song poets treated as beautiful grief.
mean: Of the nightingale; of song born from sorrow
story: Philomela was silenced and wove her story into a tapestry instead, because nobody thought to take away her loom. The gods turned her into a nightingale — the bird that sings most beautifully after dark.

who: Judge of the dead in Greek myth
why: A son of Zeus so famously just that he was made a judge in the underworld.
story: Rhadamanthus was one of three judges deciding where each soul went, and he had the reputation of being unbribable. His name is now the strongest word English has for a judge who will not bend, not even slightly.

why: She drove the moon across the night sky in a silver chariot.
story: Selene fell in love with a shepherd and asked Zeus to keep him young forever; he granted it by putting the man into eternal sleep. The element selenium is named after her, because it was found alongside one named for the earth.

why: Her name means 'delighting in dance'.
story: Terpsichore is the reason a dancer can be called a terpsichorean — a nine-letter way of saying it. Of the nine Muses she is the one whose job survives most recognisably: she is usually shown mid-step, holding a lyre.

who: Roman god of fire and the forge
why: His workshop was said to lie under Mount Etna, which explained the smoke.
story: Romans thought the rumble of Etna was Vulcan hammering underground. The island of Vulcano off Sicily was his chimney, and it gave every volcano on Earth its name — including the ones nowhere near Italy.

why: The town named the Adriatic Sea, and its adjective became a personal name.
story: A small Roman town called Hadria named the whole Adriatic Sea, then lent its adjective to the emperor Hadrian, then to popes and a great many children. The town itself is now several miles inland, left behind by the silt.

why: He carried his father out of burning Troy and sailed on to found the line that led to Rome.
story: Virgil's stock epithet for him is pius Aeneas — not pious exactly, but dutiful. He escapes Troy with his father on his back and his household gods under his arm, and spends the rest of the poem doing what he is told by fate.

why: Early Christian writers chose it over other Greek words for love to mean unconditional goodwill.
story: Greek had at least four words for love, and early Christian writers deliberately picked the least romantic one. Agape is not affection or desire — it is the kind you extend to someone who has done nothing to earn it.

why: She agreed to die in her husband's place when no one else would.
story: Admetus was allowed to escape death if someone would go instead. He asked his parents, who declined. His wife Alcestis volunteered. Heracles turned up, heard the story, and went to wrestle Death at the graveside to get her back.

why: In Moliere's play the true host is identified as the one who provides the dinner.
story: Zeus disguised himself as Amphitryon to visit his wife, producing two identical husbands and a very confused household. Moliere's version settles the question with a line the French adopted: the real Amphitryon is the one who serves the meal.

why: A rustic god of gardens and fertility, invoked to protect orchards.
story: Priapus was a garden god whose statues stood among fruit trees to frighten off birds and thieves.
skip_why: adult sense; excluded from kid-facing cards

who: Father of Aeneas in Roman myth
why: Aeneas carried his aged father out of burning Troy on his shoulders.
story: The image of Aeneas escaping Troy with his father on his back and his son by the hand became Rome's picture of duty itself — carrying the past out and leading the future forward at the same time.

why: He wrote light verse in praise of wine, music and good company.
story: A London gentlemen's club sang a drinking song called To Anacreon in Heaven. An American lawyer later set his poem about a flag to that same tune, and the United States ended up with a national anthem built on a Greek wine poet.

who: Greek term for one who withdraws
why: Early Christian hermits withdrew to the desert to live alone in prayer.
story: Anchorites went further than monks: some were sealed into a small cell attached to a church wall, with one window to the altar and one to the street, and stayed there for the rest of their lives.

why: Virgil, Horace and Ovid all wrote under him, making his reign the peak of Latin literature.
mean: Of a classical golden age in literature
story: Augustus boasted he found Rome brick and left it marble. Eighteenth-century English writers admired the period so much that they called their own era Augustan and set out to imitate it deliberately.

why: Athenians mocked their rural neighbours as slow-witted, and the slur stuck to the region's name.
story: This is an ancient insult that outlived its target. Athens sneered at Boeotia as farmland full of dullards — conveniently forgetting that Hesiod, Pindar and Plutarch all came from there.

why: Don Quixote mixes comedy and idealism so closely that neither wins.
mean: Comically idealistic in the manner of Cervantes
story: Cervantes lost the use of his left hand at the battle of Lepanto and spent five years as a captive in Algiers before writing what is often called the first modern novel. He died in the same week as Shakespeare.

why: His 1492 crossing opened sustained contact between Europe and the Americas.
mean: Of the Americas or of Columbus
story: America was named for Amerigo Vespucci, not Columbus — but Columbian survived as the poetic alternative. It is why the United States has a District of Columbia and Canada a British Columbia.

why: Too proud to court the common people, he was banished and turned his army on his own city.
story: Coriolanus could not bring himself to show his battle scars to voters, which was the custom. Exiled for the insult, he marched on Rome and was stopped only when his mother walked out to meet the army.

who: Trojan woman in medieval and Shakespearean versions of the Troy story
why: She swore constancy to Troilus and transferred her affections once she reached the Greek camp.
story: Cressida does not appear in Homer at all — she was invented in the Middle Ages and handed down through Boccaccio and Chaucer to Shakespeare, each of whom made her a little less sympathetic than the last.

who: French soldier-poet (1619-1655), immortalised in Rostand's 1897 play
why: In the play he lends his eloquence to a handsome friend, wooing the woman he loves on someone else's behalf.
mean: Eloquently romantic while hidden behind another
story: The real Cyrano wrote science fiction about travelling to the moon. Rostand gave him an enormous nose, a duelling sword, and the finest words in French theatre — all spent under a balcony, for another man.

why: His descent through the nine circles of hell set the standard for infernal imagery.
story: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in Italian rather than Latin, which scholars considered a waste of a good poem. It is the reason modern Italian sounds the way it does.

why: He lived in a large ceramic jar and owned almost nothing on principle.
story: Diogenes walked Athens in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for an honest man. When Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted, he asked him to move slightly — he was blocking the sun.

why: He read so many chivalric romances that he set out as a knight and charged windmills believing them giants.
story: Don Quixote's windmills are the most famous mistake in literature. Cervantes meant to mock outdated romances, but readers kept siding with the old man who insisted the world should be nobler than it is.

who: Greek people who settled the Peloponnese
why: Their name attached to a musical mode and to the plainest of the classical column orders.
mean: Of the Dorians; of the Doric style or mode
story: The Doric column is the plain one — no scrolls, no leaves, just fluting and a flat top. Greeks thought of it as the masculine, unfussy order, and used it for the Parthenon.

why: His geometry assumed parallel lines never meet, which held for two thousand years.
mean: Of Euclid's geometry, in which parallel lines never meet
story: Euclid's fifth postulate — about parallel lines — bothered mathematicians for centuries because it seemed like it should be provable. It is not. Dropping it produced curved, non-Euclidean geometries, and eventually general relativity.

why: The Gospels were the good news, and those who spread it were evangelists.
mean: Of the Gospel; zealously spreading a message
story: Euangelion literally means good message — in classical Greek it was the reward you gave the runner who brought good news from a battle. English kept the messenger sense in evangelist and the enthusiasm in evangelical.

who: Pope who reformed the calendar in 1582
why: The Julian year was eleven minutes too long, and by the 1500s the date had drifted ten days out of step with the seasons.
mean: Of the modern calendar or of plainsong chant
story: To fix the drift, October 1582 simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752, by which time it had to skip eleven.

why: He is a giant in one land and a doll in the next, and reports both with the same flat calm.
story: Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels as savage political satire. It was so successful as an adventure story that it turned into a children's book, which is the fate of a surprising number of angry books.

why: He rented horses strictly in rotation: you took the one nearest the door, or none at all.
mean: Of an apparent choice that is really no choice
story: Hobson had forty horses and a rule that stopped customers from wearing out the best ones. Students grumbled about Hobson's choice, and the phrase outlived every horse in the stable.

why: He wrote a dictionary almost single-handedly and spoke in weighty, balanced sentences.
story: Johnson spent nine years on his dictionary and slipped jokes into it — he defined lexicographer as a harmless drudge. His friend Boswell wrote down his conversation for years, producing the most famous biography in English.

why: He argued morality means acting only on rules you could will everyone to follow.
mean: Of Kant's philosophy of reason and duty
story: Kant kept to a schedule so exact that neighbours in Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by his afternoon walk. He never travelled more than a hundred miles from his birthplace, and rearranged Western philosophy from there.

who: Island of tiny people in Gulliver's Travels
why: Its inhabitants stood six inches tall and tied the sleeping Gulliver down with thread.
story: Lilliput's great political dispute is whether to crack a boiled egg at the big end or the little end — a war that has killed thousands. Swift was writing about religious conflict, and he was not being subtle.

who: Name meaning 'light-bringer', applied to the fallen angel
why: Pride made him rebel against heaven and fall from it.
story: Lucifer is Latin for light-bringer and was originally the morning star, Venus. A verse in Isaiah about a fallen Babylonian king was read as being about Satan, and the planet's name transferred to the devil.

why: His laws of motion and gravitation explained falling apples and orbiting planets with the same equations.
story: Newton did his best work during a plague year when Cambridge closed and he went home to the farm. In eighteen months he laid out calculus, optics and gravitation. He later called it his year of wonders.

why: He wrote hundreds of sonnets to a woman named Laura, in a form now named after him.
mean: Of the Petrarchan sonnet; of idealised unattainable love
story: Petrarch saw Laura in a church in Avignon in 1327 and wrote poems about her for the next forty years, including twenty-one after her death. There is no evidence they ever had a conversation.

why: His story of surviving alone on an island spawned an entire genre of imitations.
story: Defoe based Crusoe partly on Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish sailor marooned for four years on a Pacific island. Germans coined Robinsonade for the flood of imitations, and the genre now includes Swiss Family Robinson and Lord of the Flies.

why: Her sixty-three-year reign covered industrial expansion, empire, and a strict public code of manners.
mean: Of Victoria's reign; strait-laced and formal
story: Victoria came to the throne at eighteen and reigned longer than any British monarch before her. The word Victorian now suggests prudishness, though the queen herself wrote frankly in her diaries about how much she adored her husband.

why: Democritus was known as the laughing philosopher for his amusement at human folly.
mean: Given to constant or foolish laughter
story: Abdera produced Democritus, who worked out that matter is made of atoms twenty-three centuries early, and who reportedly could not stop laughing at people. The town's neighbours took the laughter personally.

why: Britain deported the French-speaking Acadians in 1755, and many settled in Louisiana.
story: Deported Acadians who reached Louisiana were called Acadiens, then Cadiens, then Cajuns. The whole of Cajun food, music and dialect traces back to one forced expulsion from the far north.

why: Aphrodite loved him; a boar killed him, and anemones grew where his blood fell.
mean: Strikingly handsome; also a short verse line
story: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story came west from Phoenicia. Calling a handsome man an Adonis is therefore a compliment in a language most people using it do not know.

why: An aeolian harp is played by nothing but the breeze passing over its strings.
mean: Being produced or shaped by wind
story: An aeolian harp is left in an open window and plays itself. Romantic poets loved the idea — an instrument with no performer — and used it as an image for inspiration arriving from somewhere outside you.

why: His animal fables carried their real meaning underneath the surface story.
mean: Conveying meaning indirectly, to evade censors
story: Aesop was said to be an enslaved man who won his freedom through cleverness. In Soviet Russia, Aesopian language meant writing your real point in code — because the fable was still the safest way to criticise power.

who: King of the Phaeacians in the Odyssey
why: He gave the shipwrecked Odysseus a feast, gifts and a ship home, asking nothing first.
story: Alcinous had a garden where fruit ripened all year round and never failed. He also had the good manners to feed his exhausted guest for two days before asking him who he was.

why: He led the palace school and drove the revival of learning across the Frankish empire.
story: Alcuin's scribes developed a clear rounded script called Carolingian minuscule to replace the tangle scribes had been using. Renaissance printers copied it, and the lower-case letters you are reading now descend directly from it.

who: Goat who nursed the infant Zeus
why: One of her horns broke off and filled forever with whatever its holder wished for.
story: Amalthea's broken horn became the cornucopia — the horn of plenty still drawn overflowing with fruit at harvest festivals. Zeus later set her among the stars in gratitude for the milk.

who: Egyptian god with a great temple in the Libyan desert
why: A salt collected near his temple was called sal ammoniac, and ammonia was later named from it.
story: Camel caravans camped at the temple of Amun, and a white salt crusted the ground where they did. Romans called it sal ammoniac, salt of Amun. Every bottle of ammonia is named after an Egyptian god by way of camel dung.

why: His reign was the calm centre of what Gibbon called the happiest period in human history.
mean: Of the peak of the Roman Empire
story: The Antonine Wall was built across Scotland under him, north of Hadrian's, and abandoned within about twenty years. Rome kept the older wall — the one named after the emperor who did less building.

who: Roman gourmet of the first century AD
why: The oldest surviving cookbook in the West carries his name.
story: The recipes attributed to Apicius include flamingo and dormice stuffed with pork. Legend says he poisoned himself on discovering he had only a modest fortune left and could no longer eat as he wished.

why: He coined the word surrealism and wrote poems shaped like the objects they described.
mean: Experimentally modern in the manner of Apollinaire
story: Apollinaire wrote calligrammes — poems typeset in the shape of a horse, the Eiffel Tower, falling rain. He also invented the word surrealism, three years before the movement that took it existed.

why: As librarian at Alexandria he marked doubtful lines of Homer with a severity that became proverbial.
story: Aristarchus went through Homer marking every line he thought was a later addition, using a small horizontal stroke in the margin. That stroke is the ancestor of the obelus, and the dagger symbol still used in footnotes.

why: He defined culture as the best which has been thought and said in the world.
mean: Of Arnold's view of culture as moral improvement
story: Arnold spent his working life as a school inspector, travelling England examining classrooms, and wrote criticism in the gaps. He argued that culture was the antidote to what he called anarchy, by which he mostly meant the middle classes.

who: Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare
why: She won the patronage of Athens by giving the city the olive tree.
story: Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. He struck the rock and produced a salt spring; she planted an olive tree. The citizens chose the olive, and the city took her name.

why: Athenian prose was admired for elegant plainness, and Attic came to mean refined simplicity.
mean: Elegantly simple; also a top storey
story: Attic salt means dry Athenian wit. The attic in your house is the same word: architects called a small decorative upper storey in the Athenian manner an attic storey, and the name slid up into the roof space.

who: Prince in a tale from the Arabian Nights
why: He served a starving beggar a magnificent banquet of entirely empty dishes.
mean: Illusory; generous in appearance but giving nothing
story: The Barmecide describes each imaginary course in loving detail while the beggar mimes eating it. The beggar plays along, then pretends to be drunk on imaginary wine and punches him — at which the prince laughs and serves a real dinner.

why: She guides him through Paradise in the Divine Comedy after Virgil can go no further.
mean: Of an idealised woman as spiritual guide
story: Dante met Beatrice when they were both about nine and spoke to her only a handful of times. She married someone else and died at twenty-four. He put her in charge of heaven.

why: He proposed judging every action by how much happiness it produced overall.
story: Bentham also designed the panopticon, a prison where one unseen guard could watch every cell. It was never built to his plan, but the idea has been borrowed by everyone writing about surveillance since.

why: Awaiting execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy and its image of Fortune's turning wheel.
story: Boethius wrote his masterpiece in a cell while waiting to be executed for treason. The wheel of fortune he described — lifting people up only to drop them — became the standard medieval image for how luck works.

why: He filled his canvases with crowds of peasants at work, at play and at their worst.
mean: Crowded, earthy and full of incident
story: Bruegel painted a hundred children's games in a single picture and a village wedding where you can count the pies. In his Icarus, the boy falls out of the sky and every farmer in the painting keeps working.

why: He taught that all disease came from too much or too little excitement in the body.
mean: Of Brown's theory of medical excitability
story: Brown reduced medicine to one dial: too stimulated or not stimulated enough. Treatment was opium or alcohol accordingly. It was wrong, wildly popular across Europe, and probably killed more patients than it saved.

who: King of the Franks and emperor (c. 748-814)
why: Carolus is Latin for Charles, and his dynasty and its cultural revival took the name.
mean: Of Charlemagne's dynasty and its revival of learning
story: Charlemagne ruled most of western Europe and worked at learning to write late in life, keeping a tablet under his pillow to practise. He never quite managed it, but he made sure his empire's scribes could.

why: Her prophecies were always right and never believed.
story: Apollo gave Cassandra prophecy hoping to win her affection. When she refused him he could not take the gift back, so he added a condition: she would always be right, and nobody would ever act on it.

why: He wrote short, direct, intensely personal poems about love and hatred.
mean: Intensely personal and direct in lyric
story: Catullus survives by luck — a single manuscript turned up in Verona around 1300 and vanished again after being copied. His most famous poem is two lines long and begins by saying he hates and loves at the same time.

why: Its priests were famous astronomers and astrologers, so Chaldean came to mean astrologer.
story: Chaldean astronomers kept night-sky records for centuries and could predict eclipses. Greeks and Romans used Chaldean to mean fortune-teller, which was rather like calling an astronomer a horoscope writer.

why: Italian guides who talked at length about the sights were nicknamed after the most talkative Roman.
mean: A guide who explains the sights to visitors
story: Eighteenth-century travellers on the Grand Tour hired local guides and named them ciceroni — after Cicero, whose reputation for eloquence had by then drifted into a reputation for not stopping.

why: Dismissed as a stammering fool, he proved a capable administrator who conquered Britain.
mean: Of the emperor Claudius or his period
story: Claudius survived the purges that killed the rest of his family precisely because nobody thought him worth killing. The Praetorian Guard found him hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder and made him emperor.

why: His dreamlike Kubla Khan and Ancient Mariner defined the visionary side of Romanticism.
story: Coleridge said Kubla Khan came to him complete in a dream, and that he was writing it down when a person from Porlock knocked on the door about business. By the time he got rid of the visitor, the rest of the poem was gone.

why: His tragedies turn on characters forced to choose between love and duty.
mean: Of the conflict between passion and duty
story: Corneille's Le Cid was so popular that the French Academy was pushed to condemn it for breaking the rules of classical drama. Audiences kept going anyway, and the phrase beau comme le Cid entered the language.

why: He led Parliament's army, signed a king's death warrant, and ruled without a crown.
story: Cromwell told his portrait painter to include everything, warts and all, or he would not pay for it. Two years after his death the restored monarchy dug up his body and executed it anyway.

who: Small Greek island, birthplace of Apollo
why: It was the sacred centre of an Athenian-led alliance whose treasury was kept there.
mean: Of Delos or the Delian League
story: Delos was so sacred that no one was allowed to be born or to die on it. There is also the Delian problem: an oracle demanded the islanders double a cube-shaped altar, which turns out to be impossible with compass and straightedge.

who: Greek god of wine and theatre
why: His festivals combined drinking, masks and the first performances of Greek drama.
story: Western theatre started as a religious festival for Dionysus. The plays of Sophocles and Euripides were competition entries, performed once, in an open-air theatre, at a party for the god of wine.

why: His code prescribed death for almost every offence, including stealing a cabbage.
story: Asked why the penalty for minor theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could find nothing worse for the large ones. The laws were said to be written in blood rather than ink.

why: His short reign became shorthand for the confident, elegant decade before the First World War.
mean: Of the 1900s in Britain; elegant and leisured
story: Edward waited fifty-nine years to become king — the longest apprenticeship in British history — and reigned nine. The decade named after him is remembered as one long garden party, mainly because of what came next.

why: Shakespeare, Marlowe and Spenser all wrote under her, and English sea power began in her reign.
story: Elizabeth reigned forty-four years and refused to marry throughout, telling Parliament she was already married to England. The theatre, the language and the navy all took their modern shape while she was on the throne.

why: He wore Hannibal down by delay, and British socialists took his name for gradual reform.
mean: Achieving change by patient gradual steps
story: The Fabian Society, founded in 1884, chose the name deliberately: change by patience, not revolution. Its members included George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells, and it helped found the British Labour Party.

who: Legendary warrior band of Irish myth led by Finn MacCool
why: Nineteenth-century Irish republicans took the ancient warriors' name for their movement.
story: The Fianna were mythical hunter-warriors who roamed Ireland in the old stories. When republicans organised in 1858 they reached back two thousand years for a name, which tells you how they wanted to be seen.

who: Roman name for the region that became France
why: Gallicanism was the movement to keep the French church partly independent of Rome.
story: Gaul gave French a great deal: Gallic wit, Gallicanism, and the rooster that is still France's unofficial emblem — because gallus is Latin for both a Gaul and a cockerel, and someone enjoyed the pun enough to keep it.

who: Paris building where the radical revolutionary club met
why: The club took its nickname from the address, and the name came to mean political extremism.
story: The Jacobins were named after a building, not a person — the Paris convent where they met. Under Robespierre the club drove the Terror, and Jacobin has meant dangerous radicalism in English ever since.

why: Jacobus is Latin for James, and his reign named a style of drama, furniture and Bible.
mean: Of the reign of James I
story: The King James Bible was produced under him by six committees of scholars, and its cadences shaped English prose for four centuries. Jacobean drama went the other way entirely — revenge, poison and skulls.

why: The name of the kingdom of Judah gave us both Judaea and Jew.
story: Judaea is named for Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled: from the tribe to the kingdom to the Roman province, and from there into the word Jewish.

why: He reorganised European law and warfare in twenty years and lost it all at Waterloo.
mean: Of Napoleon; boldly ambitious in scale
story: Napoleon's civil code is still the backbone of the legal system in dozens of countries. He was of perfectly ordinary height for his time — the short-Napoleon story comes from British cartoons and a confusion between French and English inches.

why: His letters make up much of the New Testament and set out much of Christian doctrine.
mean: Of the apostle Paul or his teaching
story: Paul began as Saul, a persecutor of Christians, and changed course after a blinding experience on the road to Damascus. A Damascene conversion — a sudden complete reversal — is named from that same journey.

why: He fixed an image on a silvered copper plate, producing the first practical photograph.
mean: An early photograph on a silvered plate
story: The French government bought Daguerre's process in 1839 and gave it to the world free — except in England, where he patented it. Each daguerreotype was unique: there was no negative, so no copies could be made.

why: He popularised a roof with two slopes, the lower one steep, creating a usable extra floor.
mean: A roof with a steep lower slope, giving attic space
story: Paris property was once taxed by the number of floors below the roofline, so a mansard roof added a whole storey the tax collector did not count. Good architecture and good accounting at the same time.

why: He devised a code of dots and dashes to send messages down a telegraph wire.
story: Morse was a portrait painter first. Away from home on a commission, he received a letter saying his wife was ill; by the time he got back she was already buried. He spent the rest of his life on faster messages.

why: His loom used punched cards to control the pattern automatically.
mean: Fabric woven in an intricate pattern on a Jacquard loom
story: Jacquard's loom read its pattern from a chain of punched cards. Charles Babbage saw one and borrowed the idea for his calculating engine, and punched cards ran computers into the 1970s. Modern computing starts with a French silk loom.

why: He bred a fierce, loyal guard dog to protect him on his rounds.
story: Dobermann collected taxes in a rough district and also ran the local dog pound, which gave him unusual access to breeding stock. He set out to build the perfect bodyguard, and the breed still carries his name.

who: Mistress of Louis XV of France (1721-1764)
why: She wore her hair swept high off the forehead, and the court copied her.
mean: A hairstyle with the hair swept up from the forehead
story: Madame de Pompadour was the most powerful woman at Versailles without being queen, and set fashion for two decades. Two centuries later Elvis Presley wore a version of her hairstyle, which she would probably have enjoyed.

who: Financier at the court of Louis XIV (1630-1703)
why: The white sauce was named in his honour by a court cook, probably as flattery.
mean: A white sauce of milk thickened with flour and butter
story: Bechameil was a wealthy court official, not a cook. Another courtier complained that the man was lucky — he himself had been serving the same sauce for years before Bechameil was born, and nobody had named it after him.

why: A farmer's wife there is credited with perfecting the soft cheese in the 1790s.
mean: A soft creamy cheese with a white rind
story: The story goes that Marie Harel sheltered a priest fleeing the French Revolution, and he taught her a cheesemaking method from Brie. The round wooden box came later, and is why Camembert could travel.

why: The blue cheese must be aged in the natural limestone caves beneath the village.
story: Only cheese ripened in the caves of one specific village may be called Roquefort — a protection first granted by royal charter in 1411, making it one of the oldest brand protections in the world.

why: Brandy distilled from grapes grown around the town takes its name.
mean: A fine brandy from the Cognac region
story: All cognac is brandy, but only brandy from around this one town may be called cognac. The rule is strict enough that even neighbouring Armagnac, made a hundred miles away, has to use its own name.

why: Only sparkling wine from that region may legally carry the name.
mean: Sparkling wine from the Champagne region
story: The region's name comes from the Latin campania, meaning open country. The bubbles were originally an accident and considered a fault — the cold Champagne winters stopped fermentation, which restarted in spring inside the sealed bottle.

why: The deep red of its wine gave English a colour name.
mean: A deep purplish red; wine from Burgundy
story: Burgundy is one of a small group of colours named after drinks — along with claret and port. The region itself is named for the Burgundians, a Germanic people who settled there around 1,500 years ago.

why: Fine translucent porcelain reached Europe from China and took the country's name.
story: Europeans spent centuries trying to work out how the Chinese made porcelain so thin that light passed through it. The recipe was finally cracked in Saxony in 1708, but by then the tableware was permanently called china.

why: The city was the great medieval trading centre for patterned woven silk.
mean: A rich patterned fabric woven with a reversible design
story: Damascus gave English three words: damask for the cloth, damascene for patterned steel and inlaid metal, and damson for the plum. All three arrived along the same trade routes.

why: The tough cotton twill was serge de Nimes — serge from Nimes — shortened in English to denim.
story: Your jeans are named after two European cities at once. The fabric is de Nimes, from Nimes in France. The trousers are from Genoa in Italy, which the French called Genes — which English turned into jeans.

why: The fine underwool of Himalayan goats was first woven into shawls there.
mean: Very fine soft wool from the cashmere goat
story: Cashmere is not the goat's outer coat but the soft underlayer it grows for winter, combed out by hand in spring. One goat yields a few ounces a year, which is why a cashmere jumper costs what it does.

who: Old name for Ankara, capital of Turkey
why: The long-haired goats, rabbits and cats of the region were all named after the city.
mean: Wool from the angora goat or rabbit
story: Angora names three different animals — a goat, a rabbit and a cat — all long-haired, all from around Ankara. Confusingly, the goat's wool is sold as mohair, and only the rabbit's is sold as angora.

why: European traders first met the fine cotton cloth there and named it for the city.
mean: A lightweight loosely woven cotton cloth
story: The finest muslin actually came from Bengal, where weavers produced cloth so sheer it was nicknamed woven air. Europeans met it in Mosul first, so the Iraqi city got the credit and the name.

who: Port city in Kerala, India, now Kozhikode
why: Printed cotton shipped from the port took its name across Europe.
story: Calico was so popular in England that in 1721 Parliament banned it outright to protect the wool trade. The ban lasted thirty-three years and made smuggling printed cotton genuinely profitable.

why: The ribbed crepe fabric took the French name for Moroccan.
story: Marocain is simply French for Moroccan. It is one of several fabrics that arrived in Europe with a nationality attached and kept it, alongside morocco leather from the same country.

why: Its leatherworkers produced a prized fine leather in the Middle Ages.
mean: A fine leather, originally from Cordoba
story: Cordoba's leather was so famous that the workers who made shoes from it were called cordwainers — a word still used for shoemakers in Britain, six centuries after the trade with Spain dried up.

why: French shops sold gants de Suede, Swedish gloves, made of soft napped leather.
mean: Leather with a soft napped finish
story: Suede is just the French word for Sweden. Parisians bought Swedish gloves made from the underside of the skin rather than the smooth outer face, and English took the country's name for the texture.

who: Last king of Illyria (2nd century BC)
why: He was said to have discovered the medicinal value of the plant's bitter root.
mean: A mountain plant with vivid blue flowers
story: Gentius lost his kingdom to Rome and was paraded through the streets as a captive. His one lasting monument is a small blue alpine flower, named because he supposedly found a use for its extraordinarily bitter root.

why: He was physician to James I of England, and the plant was named in his honour.
mean: A garden plant with small blue or red flowers
story: De l'Obel tried to classify plants by the shape of their leaves, which was wrong but useful — it was one of the first attempts to sort plants by their structure rather than by whether they were edible.

why: The shrub is poisonous to livestock, so the flattering name was a superstitious precaution.
mean: A shrub with bright autumn foliage and berries
story: The name means good name or lucky name — given precisely because the plant is poisonous to cattle. Farmers named it something pleasant in the hope of not attracting bad luck. It is also called the spindle tree.

why: French naturalists in Brazil noticed the flower resembled tobacco and borrowed the local name.
mean: A garden plant with funnel-shaped flowers
story: Petunia is not named after a person or a place but after a plant it merely resembles. Petun is the Tupi word for tobacco, and petunias and tobacco really are close relatives — both in the nightshade family.

who: Channel Island between England and France
why: The island's knitted woollen garments and its dairy cattle both took its name.
mean: A knitted garment; a breed of dairy cow
story: Jersey knitting was originally what fishermen wore. The island also gave its name to a small fawn-coloured cow prized for creamy milk, and to a large American state that needed a name in 1664.

why: A smooth linen cloth exported from there kept the name in English.
mean: A smooth linen or cotton fabric
story: Holland cloth was the standard lining and window-blind fabric for centuries. The region also gave English the Dutch oven, Dutch courage and going Dutch — mostly coined by the English during periods of naval rivalry.

why: The sheer crinkled silk she popularised took her first name.
mean: A thin crinkled silk or crepe fabric
story: Georgette is one of very few fabrics named after a woman, and one of fewer still named by first name rather than surname. The crinkle comes from twisting the yarn hard in opposite directions before weaving.

why: Its lacemakers produced a fine bobbin lace with a distinctive diamond mesh.
story: Valenciennes lace was so slow to make that a skilled worker might produce an inch and a half in a day, and only in a cool damp cellar — dry air made the linen thread snap.

why: It was the leading medieval centre for woven wall tapestries.
story: An arras hung a little away from the wall, which made it useful for eavesdropping. Polonius hides behind one in Hamlet to listen in, and Hamlet stabs straight through the cloth.

why: Its smiths inlaid steel with gold and silver in flowing patterns; also the site of Paul's conversion.
mean: Inlaid with wavy patterns; or a sudden total change of view
story: Damascene carries two unrelated senses from the same city: watered patterns in steel, and a Damascene conversion — a sudden reversal of belief, from the apostle Paul's experience on the road there.

why: The small dark plum was the damascene plum, shortened over time to damson.
story: Damson is Damascus worn down by centuries of English mouths: damascenum, damascene, damson. The Romans carried the tree west, and it grows in English hedgerows now as if it had always been there.

who: Port on the island of Menorca
why: French forces captured the port in 1756, and the sauce is said to have been named for the victory.
mean: A thick cold sauce of egg yolk and oil
story: The usual story credits the Duke of Richelieu's cook, improvising a sauce after taking Port Mahon in 1756. Rival theories point to the town of Bayonne or to the French word for egg yolk. Nobody can settle it.

why: The large smooth sausage of the city gave American English its lunch meat.
story: Bologna's own mortadella is studded with pistachios and cubes of fat. The American version dropped nearly all of that, kept the name, and pronounced it baloney — which then became a word for nonsense.

why: The hard aged cheese comes from Parma and the surrounding provinces.
mean: A hard, sharp, aged Italian cheese
story: Real Parmigiano-Reggiano ages at least a year, and each wheel is tested by a man who taps it with a small hammer and listens. Wheels that sound wrong inside are marked and sold under a different name.

who: Southern Italian cheese name, from a word meaning a round shape
why: Provolone is the large version of the older provola cheese of Campania.
mean: A firm smooth Italian cheese, often smoked
story: Provolone means big provola. It is a pasta filata cheese — the curd is heated and stretched like dough until it turns glossy, the same technique that makes mozzarella, then hung in ropes to age.

why: Its fortified wine survived long sea voyages and improved in the heat.
story: Madeira was discovered to taste better after crossing the tropics twice in a hot ship's hold. Producers began heating it deliberately. American revolutionaries toasted the Declaration of Independence with it.

why: The plain butter sponge was named not for its ingredients but for the wine served alongside it.
mean: A plain rich butter sponge cake
story: There is no Madeira in Madeira cake. Nineteenth-century English hosts served the plain sponge with a glass of Madeira wine in the middle of the morning, and the cake ended up named after the drink.

why: Cuban cigars shipped from the port became the standard of quality.
story: Havana cigars are rolled from tobacco grown in the Vuelta Abajo valley, where the soil and humidity are considered impossible to reproduce. Rollers traditionally worked while a reader read novels aloud to the room.

why: The soft white mineral is so light that it floats, and was imagined to be foam turned to stone.
mean: A soft white mineral used for tobacco pipes
story: Not named for a person or a place but for what sailors thought it was: lumps of white mineral washing up light enough to float, so obviously sea foam gone solid. It carves beautifully, which is why pipes were made of it.

why: The thin smoked sausage of Frankfurt travelled to America with German emigrants.
mean: A thin smoked sausage; a hot dog
story: Frankfurt has been making this sausage since the 1400s. German emigrants brought it to America, where it met a bread roll — and the frankfurter became the hot dog, named by someone who thought the shape looked like a dachshund.

who: Capital of Austria, Wien in German
why: Wiener simply means Viennese, and the sausage is Vienna's version.
story: Vienna and Frankfurt both claim the sausage, and each named it after the other city: Austrians call it a Frankfurter, Germans call it a Wiener. The man who first made it had trained in Frankfurt and moved to Vienna.

who: City in Bohemia, now the Czech Republic
why: The world's first pale golden lager was brewed there in 1842.
story: Before 1842 nearly all beer was dark and cloudy. Plzen's brewers dumped thirty-six barrels of bad beer in the street, hired a Bavarian brewer, and produced a clear golden lager. Most beer in the world today is a copy of it.

why: Monks at the town's monastery made the strong-smelling cheese; the name comes from monasterium.
story: Munster is a worn-down form of monasterium, the Latin for monastery — so the cheese is really called monastery cheese. Irish Munster is a different word entirely, from an old Irish tribal name.

who: Historic duchy now split between Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany
why: The cheese was first made by monks in the region.
mean: A soft cheese with a very strong smell
story: Limburger's smell comes from a bacterium that also lives on human skin. Researchers have shown that mosquitoes attracted to human feet are equally attracted to a piece of Limburger, which says something about both.

why: The mild cheese was traded from the town's port in distinctive round red-waxed balls.
mean: A mild Dutch cheese in a red wax coating
story: Edam ages slowly and barely spoils, which made it the standard cheese for long sea voyages. Dutch ships carried it worldwide, and its red wax shell is really just very effective packaging.

why: The cheese was not made there but traded at the town's market, which held the exclusive rights.
story: Gouda is named for a marketplace, not a dairy. The town held the sole right to trade cheese in the region, so every wheel that passed through took the town's name regardless of which farm made it.

why: The cheese was originally matured in the caves of Cheddar Gorge, where the temperature stays constant.
story: Cheddar Gorge's caves stay at a steady cool temperature all year, which is exactly what the cheese needs. Cheddar is now the most-eaten cheese in the world, and almost none of it comes from Cheddar.

why: The cheese was never made in Stilton — it was sold to travellers at the village coaching inn.
story: Stilton is named after a village where it was never produced. Coaches on the Great North Road stopped at the Bell Inn there, the landlord sold cheese from Leicestershire to passengers, and they named it after the stop.

why: Two chemists in Worcester made the fermented sauce in 1837, from a recipe they found unpleasant at first.
story: Lea and Perrill mixed the first batch, tasted it, hated it, and left the barrel in the cellar. Eighteen months later they tried it again out of curiosity. Fermentation had transformed it, and they started selling it immediately.

why: The pepper variety used in the sauce carried the state's name.
mean: A very hot sauce made from tabasco peppers
story: Tabasco sauce has been made on the same Louisiana island since 1868, aged three years in oak barrels with salt from the salt dome beneath. The pepper — and therefore the name — came from Mexico.

who: Town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolivar
why: A German army surgeon there developed the bitters in 1824 as a stomach remedy for soldiers.
mean: An aromatic bitters used in drinks
story: Dr Siegert made his bitters as medicine for Simon Bolivar's troops. The town changed its name to Ciudad Bolivar in 1846 and the company later moved to Trinidad, so the bottle now names a place that no longer exists.

who: City in Germany, Koln in German
why: An Italian perfumer created eau de Cologne there in 1709.
story: Giovanni Maria Farina created his scent in Cologne and wrote that it reminded him of an Italian spring morning after rain. His company still exists — arguably the oldest perfume house in the world.

why: Literally 'water of Cologne', the original name of Farina's 1709 scent.
mean: A light perfume of citrus oils in alcohol
story: Napoleon's soldiers took eau de Cologne home in such quantities that it became the standard word for light perfume across Europe. Napoleon himself is said to have used a bottle a day.

why: A vivid new aniline dye was named for a French victory fought there in 1859.
story: The dye was discovered in the same year as the Battle of Magenta and named to ride the news. It is one of the four printing inks — every colour photo ever printed uses a colour named after a battlefield.

why: Another 1859 battle in the same campaign gave its name to a second new dye colour.
story: Solferino's real legacy is not the colour. A Swiss traveller named Henry Dunant saw forty thousand casualties left untended after the battle, wrote a book about it, and founded the Red Cross.

who: British island territory in the Atlantic
why: Knee-length shorts became acceptable business dress there in the island's heat.
story: Bermuda shorts began as British army tropical kit and became ordinary office wear on the island — worn with a jacket, tie and knee socks. It is still normal business dress in Bermuda.

who: Port city in Italy, Genes in French
why: A tough cotton fustian made there was called jene fustian in English, shortened to jean.
mean: Heavy cotton twill; trousers made from it
story: Genoese sailors wore trousers of this hard-wearing cloth, and the French called the city Genes. English heard jean. The cloth in modern jeans is denim, from Nimes, so the garment is named after two cities at once.

who: Hindi word meaning variegated or speckled
why: Printed Indian cottons reached Europe under their Indian name, pluralised in English to chintz.
mean: Printed glazed cotton with a floral pattern
story: Chintz is a rare case of an English singular made from a foreign plural — chints was the plural of chint. It was so fashionable, then so common, that chintzy came to mean cheap and gaudy.

why: The cloth reached Europe through Malay traders and kept its Malay name.
mean: A checked or striped cotton cloth
story: Gingham was originally striped, not checked — the checks arrived later in Manchester mills. The name is Malay, one of a handful of everyday English words that came by ship from Southeast Asia.

why: A coarse ribbed woollen cloth was woven there from the fourteenth century.
story: Kersey is a village of a few hundred people that named a cloth traded across medieval Europe. Along with worsted from Norfolk, it is a reminder that English wool towns once set the standard for the continent.

why: Flemish weavers settled there and produced a smooth yarn from long combed wool.
mean: Smooth yarn or cloth made from long combed wool
story: Worstead is now a quiet village, but in the Middle Ages its cloth funded the enormous churches that still stand across Norfolk — buildings far too large for the parishes that own them.

why: The Arabic name for the fine goat-hair cloth was reshaped in English as if it contained the word hair.
mean: A fabric made from angora goat hair
story: Mohair only looks like it contains the word hair. It is Arabic mukhayyar, meaning select cloth, which English speakers reshaped into something that sounded like it made sense. That process is called folk etymology.

why: Goatskin tanned with sumac in Morocco produced a soft durable leather prized for bookbinding.
story: Morocco leather was the standard for fine bookbinding for centuries — soft enough to work, strong enough to last. The best grade is still called levant morocco, after another region entirely.

why: A fine silk net for veils and gowns was first made there.
mean: A fine silk or nylon net fabric
story: Tulle is the stuff of every ballet skirt and wedding veil. The town that named it is a quiet place in the Correze that most French people associate with something else entirely — it is also a former presidential hometown.

why: A thin transparent cloth traded through the city is thought to have taken its name.
story: The Gaza origin is the traditional explanation, though some scholars trace gauze to an Arabic word for raw silk instead. Either way it arrived in Europe along Mediterranean trade routes with its name attached.

why: The crisp sheer cotton is thought to be named for the Silk Road city that traded it.
story: Organdy is the crispest cotton made — the stiffness comes from treating the woven cloth with acid. Its name most likely travelled the Silk Road from Urgench, a city few English speakers have ever heard of.

why: Its potters imitated Chinese porcelain in blue on white tin-glazed earthenware.
story: Delft potters were copying Chinese porcelain they could not chemically reproduce, so they faked it: white tin glaze over ordinary clay, painted blue. The imitation became famous in its own right and outlived the thing it imitated.

why: Tin-glazed Spanish pottery reached Italy via Majorca and took the island's name.
story: Majolica is named for a stopover, not a source. The pottery was Spanish, but it reached Italian buyers through Majorca, and Italians named it after the island the ships came from.

why: French buyers named the tin-glazed pottery after the Italian city that supplied it.
story: Faience and majolica are nearly the same pottery named by two different countries after two different middlemen — the French said Faenza, the Italians said Majorca. Both were describing tin-glazed earthenware.

who: London street and market carriers of the eighteenth century
why: The strong dark beer was popular with the men who hauled goods around the city.
story: Porter is named after its drinkers rather than a person or place — the porters who carried loads through London markets. Extra-strong porter was called stout porter, which is where stout comes from.

why: An English merchant began fortifying the local wine in 1773 so it would survive shipping.
story: John Woodhouse's ship sheltered at Marsala, he tasted the local wine, and he added spirit so it would survive the voyage to England. Sicily got an export industry out of one storm.

why: English traders pronounced Jerez as sherris, then took it for a plural and made a singular from it.
mean: A fortified wine from southern Spain
story: English merchants heard Jerez, said sherris, assumed the s meant plural, and invented sherry as the singular. The same mistake gave English pea from pease and cherry from cerise.

why: Medieval Bordeaux wine was lighter in colour than modern red, so the English called it clairet.
story: Claret describes a colour, not a place — the pale red of medieval Bordeaux, which was closer to today's rose. English drinkers kept the word even after the wine got much darker.

who: Region of Gascony in southwest France
why: Brandy distilled there predates cognac by about two centuries.
mean: A brandy from the Armagnac region
story: Armagnac is older than cognac and distilled only once rather than twice, which leaves more flavour and less polish. It is made in far smaller quantities, largely because Armagnac has no river to the sea.

why: The straw hats were woven in Ecuador but shipped through Panama, so buyers named them for the port.
story: Panama hats are Ecuadorian. They were shipped through Panama, and when Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the canal works in 1906, the wrong name stuck permanently to a hat from another country.

why: He showed that gently heating liquids killed the microbes that spoiled them.
mean: To heat a liquid briefly to destroy harmful microbes
story: Pasteur was asked to find out why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it, and that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Milk got the same treatment, and childhood deaths dropped.

who: Roman goddess of grain and harvest
why: Grain crops were her gift, and Roman festivals in her honour celebrated the harvest.
mean: A grain crop; breakfast food made from grain
story: Your breakfast is named after a Roman goddess. Ceres governed grain and the harvest, and the Romans called the crops themselves cerealia — her things. Four thousand years later it is written on a cardboard box.

why: He was quick, clever and impossible to pin down, and the metal named after him behaves the same way.
story: Mercury had winged sandals and never stayed anywhere long. The only liquid metal was named after him for the same reason — it rolls away the moment you touch it. A mercurial person is just as hard to hold.

who: Roman god of fire and the forge
why: Romans believed the smoking island of Vulcano was the chimney of his underground workshop.
mean: A mountain that erupts molten rock
story: There is a small Italian island called Vulcano, named for the god the Romans thought was hammering away beneath it. Every volcano on Earth — and on Mars — is named after one god's forge.

why: He designed a shell packed with musket balls that burst in mid-air over enemy troops.
mean: Fragments scattered by an exploding shell
story: Shrapnel spent his own money developing the shell and worked on it for years before the army adopted it in 1803. He got a pension and a word in every language. It is not the legacy most people would choose.

why: His dramatic side whiskers were called burnsides, and people later flipped the halves of the word.
mean: Strips of facial hair grown down the sides of the face
story: They were called burnsides first, after the general who wore an enormous pair. Somewhere along the way English swapped the two halves and produced sideburns — which now sounds like it describes the sides, purely by accident.

why: His followers resisted new Renaissance learning, so reformers turned his name into an insult.
story: Duns Scotus was one of the sharpest minds of the Middle Ages. When fashions in learning changed, his stubborn followers were mocked as Dunses — and one of the cleverest men of his age ended up meaning the opposite.

why: He wrote about cruelty at length and spent much of his life imprisoned.
story: De Sade spent roughly thirty-two years locked up, and wrote much of his work in prison — including one novel on a continuous roll of paper hidden in his cell wall. A psychiatrist coined sadism from his name in 1886.

why: His novel Venus in Furs described a man who found pleasure in being dominated.
mean: Taking pleasure in one's own suffering
story: Sacher-Masoch was a respected historian and novelist who deeply resented having his name turned into a clinical term. The psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing coined it anyway, and paired it with sadism in the same book.

why: He was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, producing accidental nonsense.
mean: A slip in which the first sounds of words are swapped
story: Spooner is supposed to have toasted our queer old dean instead of our dear old queen. Most of the famous examples were probably invented by students, but he really did make the slips — and only ever admitted to one.

why: He crossed a raspberry, blackberry and loganberry, then abandoned the vines when his farm failed.
mean: A large dark berry crossed from several species
story: Boysen gave up and left his experimental vines to die. Walter Knott tracked down the last few survivors on the abandoned farm, nursed them back, and named the berry after the man who had quit.

why: His cook coated almonds in caramelised sugar and named the sweet after his employer.
mean: A sweet of nuts in caramelised sugar
story: The cook, Clement Lassagne, is said to have invented the sweet after watching a kitchen boy eat spilled caramel and almonds. He named it for his employer, opened a shop, and the shop still exists in Montargis.

why: A Naples pizzaiolo made her a pizza in the colours of the new Italian flag: red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil.
mean: A pizza of tomato, mozzarella and basil
story: In 1889 Raffaele Esposito made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the patriotic one, and he named it after her. Whether the story is strictly true is argued over, but the pizza is definitely named for a queen.

why: The bacterium was isolated in his laboratory and named for him, though his assistant did the work.
story: Theobald Smith actually identified the organism. Salmon was his supervisor, and the naming followed the rank rather than the work — an old habit in science. Salmon was the first person in America to earn a veterinary doctorate.

why: He pioneered antiseptic surgery, and the bacterium was named in his honour.
story: Lister worked out that infection came from invisible organisms and started spraying carbolic acid in operating theatres. Death rates collapsed. He has a bacterium named after him and, less flatteringly, a mouthwash.

why: Finns mocked his claim that Soviet bombs were food parcels, and named their petrol bombs a drink to go with the bread.
mean: A petrol bomb in a bottle
story: Molotov said Soviet aircraft were dropping food to starving Finns. The Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets — and named their own petrol bombs Molotov cocktails, a drink to go with the meal.

why: He built the tube that clicks when it detects a particle of radiation.
story: Geiger's first counters had to be watched, hour after hour, counting flashes on a screen in a dark room. He built the clicking tube partly so that physicists could stop staring and start listening.

why: He devised a scale that measures earthquake size on a logarithmic curve.
story: Each whole step up the Richter scale is about thirty-two times more energy released — so a magnitude 7 is not slightly worse than a 6, it is thirty-two times worse. Richter built his scale for California and it went worldwide.

why: Engineers named the unit of sound intensity the bel after him; a decibel is one tenth of it.
story: The bel turned out to be too big for everyday use, so almost nobody uses it — we use tenths. Bell's mother and wife were both deaf, and his work on sound began as work on teaching deaf children to speak.

why: The clean, hot, adjustable gas flame is named after him, though his technician built it.
mean: A gas burner giving a hot clean flame
story: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built the burner to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen also lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and nearly died twice of arsenic poisoning. Chemistry was more dangerous then.

why: Working for Robert Koch, he devised the shallow lidded dish for growing cultures.
mean: A shallow lidded dish for growing microbes
story: Before Petri, cultures were grown on plates under bell jars that had to be lifted, letting in whatever was floating past. His two-part dish with an overlapping lid solved contamination with almost no moving parts.

why: During the American Revolution he ran an unofficial court that punished suspects without proper trial.
story: Lynch's court handed out floggings, not hangings — the killing sense came later and much worse. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and turned into a word for one of America's darkest habits.

who: Roman god of doorways and beginnings
why: He had two faces, one looking back and one looking forward, which suits the turn of the year.
mean: The first month of the year
story: Janus guarded doorways and had a face on each side, so he could see where you had been and where you were going at the same time. That is exactly what people do on the first of January.

why: March was when the campaigning season opened and armies marched out again.
mean: The third month of the year
story: March was once the first month of the Roman year — the point where winter ended and armies could move again. That is also why September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

who: Roman goddess of growth and spring
why: Her festival fell at the start of the month when plants grow fastest.
mean: The fifth month of the year
story: Maia was a goddess of growing things, and her month is when growth is at its fastest. She was also the mother of Mercury, which makes May and mercurial distant relatives.

who: Roman queen of the gods, protector of marriage
why: Her month was considered the luckiest time to marry.
mean: The sixth month of the year
story: Juno looked after marriage, so Romans thought June the luckiest month for a wedding. Two thousand years later June is still the most popular wedding month in much of the world, for a reason almost nobody remembers.

who: Roman god of agriculture and time
why: It is the only English weekday still named after a Roman god rather than a Norse one.
mean: The seventh day of the week
story: Saturday is the odd one out. The Anglo-Saxons swapped most Roman gods for their own — Mars became Tiw, Jupiter became Thor — but nobody found a match for Saturn, so he kept his day.

why: Thor's day replaced the Roman day of Jupiter, who was also a thunder god.
mean: The fifth day of the week
story: The Romans called it Jupiter's day; the Anglo-Saxons had their own thunder god and swapped him in. In French it is still jeudi, from Jove — so the same day is named after two different thunder gods in two languages.

why: Her day replaced the Roman day of Venus, goddess of love.
mean: The sixth day of the week
story: Friday matches Frigg to Venus — love goddess for love goddess. French kept the Roman version as vendredi. English took the Norse one, which is why our week is a mixture of two different mythologies.

who: Norse and Germanic god of war, also called Tyr
why: Tiw's day replaced the Roman day of Mars.
mean: The third day of the week
story: Tyr lost his hand feeding it to a giant wolf as a pledge, knowing the pledge was a lie — the bravest act in Norse myth. His day is the plain-sounding Tuesday, which does not hint at any of that.

who: Anglo-Saxon name for Odin, chief Norse god
why: Woden's day replaced the Roman day of Mercury.
mean: The fourth day of the week
story: Wednesday is Woden's day, and the silent d is the fossil of the missing name. Odin gave an eye for wisdom and hung from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes — none of which survives in the spelling except that d.

who: Wealthy village in New York State
why: A member of its country club wore a short dinner jacket instead of tails in 1886, and the style took the club's name.
story: Tuxedo Park is named from a Lenape word, probably meaning something like crooked river. So the most formal jacket in English is named after a New York country club named after a Native American place name.

why: The low cushioned seat came to Europe from Ottoman Turkey and took the empire's name.
mean: A low padded seat or footstool without a back
story: An empire that lasted six hundred years is now best known in English homes as a padded footstool. Osman's dynasty ruled from the Balkans to Arabia, and the furniture is what English kept of the name.

why: He is said to have worn a coat with the tails burnt off, and the cropped jacket caught on.
story: One story says his coat-tails caught fire at a fireplace and he simply had them cut off. Another says he lost a bet. Either way the cropped jacket became fashionable and has come back roughly once a century since.

why: His hoisting gallows design gave its name first to the gallows and then to any lifting crane.
story: Derrick was a convicted criminal pardoned on condition that he become the hangman. His gallows used a pivoting beam and pulley, and oil rigs use the same shape and the same name four hundred years later.

why: His hotels in Paris and London set the standard for luxury, and his name became the adjective.
story: Ritz was fired from his first restaurant job for being unsuited to the trade. He went on to run the Savoy, open the Paris Ritz, and put his name into English twice — as ritzy and in putting on the Ritz.

why: He invented a written syllabary for Cherokee, and the giant tree was named in his honour.
mean: A giant redwood tree of California
story: Sequoyah could not read any language when he began, and worked for twelve years to build a writing system from scratch. Within a few years most of the Cherokee nation was literate. The largest trees on Earth carry his name.

why: The climbing plant was collected on his round-the-world voyage and named for him.
mean: A climbing plant with bright papery bracts
story: The plant was probably first described by Jeanne Baret, the expedition's botanist's assistant, who sailed disguised as a man and became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe. The plant is named after the captain.

why: He sent specimens of the small fish to the British Museum, which named it after him.
mean: A small brightly coloured freshwater fish
story: The guppy had already been described and named twice before Guppy sent his specimens, so his name is not the official scientific one. It is the one everybody actually uses, which he probably would have settled for.

why: He crossed a blackberry with a raspberry in his garden, by accident.
mean: A dark red berry crossed from blackberry and raspberry
story: Logan was trying to breed better blackberries and planted his varieties too close to a raspberry. The bees did the rest. He was a judge by profession and got a fruit named after him for a gardening mistake.

why: The small seedless citrus was found in his orphanage garden and named for him.
mean: A small sweet seedless citrus fruit
story: Brother Clement ran an orphanage outside Oran and noticed one tree in the garden producing unusually sweet, seedless fruit. It was a chance hybrid. Every clementine sold today descends from that single accidental tree.

why: The seedless mandarin was brought to the West from that province in the 1870s.
mean: A seedless variety of mandarin orange
