story: The wife of an American ambassador sent trees home from Satsuma province in 1878 and the name travelled with them. In Japan the same fruit is called mikan — nobody there calls it a satsuma.

why: The small orange was shipped to Europe and America through Tangier.
story: Tangerines are named for the port they were shipped from, not where they grew — the fruit is originally Chinese. It is the same pattern as the Panama hat: the name records the harbour, not the home.

why: Melon seeds from Armenia were reportedly first grown in Europe on the estate.
story: Cantalupo means something like wolf-song. The melon came from Armenia by way of a papal garden, and the sweet orange fruit in your fruit salad is named after a place where wolves were once heard howling.

why: He asked for a tuba that wrapped around the player and pointed forward for marching bands.
mean: A large brass instrument coiled around the player
story: Sousa wanted a bass instrument that would carry sound over a marching band rather than up into the sky. He wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever too, so he is one of very few people who named both an instrument and an anthem.

why: He built an instrument played by moving the hands near two antennas, without touching it.
mean: An electronic instrument played without contact
story: Theremin invented his instrument by accident while building a proximity sensor. He later designed a Soviet listening device that hung inside the American embassy for seven years, powered by nothing but the radio beam aimed at it.

why: His instruments have never been convincingly matched, and his Latinised name marks them.
story: Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments and around 650 survive. Scientists have tested the varnish, the wood density, even the effect of a colder climate on the trees, and still cannot agree on why they sound the way they do.

why: He anglicised his name to Steinway after emigrating, and it became the mark of the concert grand.
mean: A piano made by Steinway and Sons
story: Steinweg built his first piano in his kitchen in Germany as a wedding gift for his wife. He emigrated in 1850, changed the name to Steinway because it sounded better in English, and the firm holds well over a hundred patents.

why: He built the first widely used voltage-controlled music synthesizer.
story: Moog started out building theremin kits as a teenager. His synthesizer reached the public through a 1968 album of Bach played entirely on it, which went platinum and put an electronic instrument in ordinary living rooms.

why: He measured the force between electric charges and the unit of charge took his name.
mean: The SI unit of electric charge
story: Coulomb measured forces far too small to feel by hanging a rod from a fine thread and watching how far it twisted. The same delicate trick was later used to weigh the Earth.

why: He discovered electromagnetic induction, and the unit of capacitance carries his name.
story: Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the greatest experimentalist of the century, and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.

why: His equations unified electricity, magnetism and light; a unit of magnetic flux bears his name.
story: Maxwell's four equations showed that light is an electromagnetic wave — arguably the single greatest leap in physics between Newton and Einstein. Einstein kept a photograph of him on his study wall.

why: He pioneered radiation dosimetry, and the unit of absorbed radiation dose is named for him.
mean: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose
story: Gray worked out how to measure exactly how much radiation a tissue absorbs — the difference between a useful cancer treatment and a lethal exposure. It is a rare unit that is genuinely a matter of life and death.

why: He mapped the solar spectrum in units of one ten-billionth of a metre.
mean: A unit of length equal to one ten-billionth of a metre
story: An angstrom is about the width of a hydrogen atom, which makes it the natural ruler for anything atomic. Angstrom also found hydrogen in the Sun, using nothing but the colours in its light.

why: He studied shock waves from supersonic projectiles, and the speed-of-sound ratio took his name.
mean: The ratio of speed to the speed of sound
story: Mach photographed a bullet in flight in 1887 and captured the shock wave coming off it — the first evidence anyone had seen. Mach 1 is not a fixed speed: sound travels slower in cold air, so it changes with altitude.

who: Irish hydrographer and Royal Navy officer (1774-1857)
why: He devised a wind scale defined by what sailors could observe rather than by instruments.
mean: A scale of wind force from 0 to 12
story: Beaufort's scale needed no instruments at all — each step is described by what the sea and the sails are doing. Force 12 was originally defined as that which no canvas could withstand.

why: He developed the first effective polio vaccine and refused to patent it.
story: Asked who owned the patent, Salk said the people did — could you patent the sun? Forgoing the patent may have cost him billions. Polio cases in the United States fell from around 58,000 a year to almost none.

why: He described the abdominal thrust that clears an obstructed airway.
mean: An abdominal thrust to dislodge a blocked airway
story: Heimlich published the technique in 1974 and it was in use within weeks. He was ninety-six when he reportedly used it himself for the first time in an emergency, on a fellow resident of his retirement home.

why: She devised a five-point check scored on every newborn one minute after birth.
mean: A quick health score given to newborn babies
story: Apgar wrote her five checks on a scrap of paper in a hospital cafeteria when a student asked how to assess a newborn quickly. It is now performed on virtually every baby born in a hospital anywhere.

why: He popularised overlapping circles as a way of showing how sets relate.
mean: A diagram of overlapping circles showing set relations
story: Venn called them Eulerian circles and never claimed to have invented them — versions appear centuries earlier. He did build a cricket bowling machine that clean bowled a visiting Australian team, which he may have preferred to be known for.

why: He invented dynamite and left his fortune to fund prizes for benefit to humanity.
mean: The international prizes funded by Nobel's estate
story: A French paper mistakenly printed Nobel's obituary while he was alive, under the headline The Merchant of Death Is Dead. He read his own reputation, disliked it, and rewrote his will to fund the prizes.

why: He endowed prizes for journalism and letters in his will.
mean: An American prize for journalism and writing
story: Pulitzer arrived in America as a penniless immigrant recruited into the Union army, and ended up owning New York's biggest paper. He also helped pay for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal by shaming his readers into donating.

who: Nickname of the Academy Award statuette
why: Nobody is certain who first said it looked like their Uncle Oscar, and the Academy adopted the name in 1939.
story: Three people claimed to have named it, all saying the statuette reminded them of someone called Oscar. The Academy could not settle the argument, gave up, and made the nickname official.

why: He created the first fully synthetic plastic and named it after himself.
story: Bakelite was the first plastic made from nothing that had ever been alive — no plant, no insect, entirely synthetic. Baekeland had already made a fortune inventing photographic paper, and could afford to experiment.

who: Plain in Greece, site of a battle in 490 BC
why: A runner is said to have carried news of the Greek victory to Athens and died on arrival.
mean: A long-distance race of about 42 kilometres
story: The modern distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box — which is why every marathon since has been an oddly specific 42.195 kilometres.

who: Greek hero whose sacred grove stood outside Athens
why: Plato taught in that grove, and his school took the name of the ground it stood on.
mean: A place of learning or a society of scholars
story: Plato's school met in an olive grove sacred to a half-forgotten hero named Akademos. It ran for nearly nine hundred years, and every academy, academic and academia traces back to that one patch of ground.

who: Follower of Jesus in the Gospels
why: Painters showed her weeping, and her name — pronounced maudlin in English — became the word for tearful sentimentality.
story: Medieval English pronounced Magdalene as maudlin, which is why two Oxford and Cambridge colleges spelled Magdalen are still said that way. Centuries of paintings of her in tears did the rest.

why: Hymns of thanksgiving sung to him became the word for any song of praise.
mean: A song of praise or triumph
story: Paean was the doctor who patched the gods up when they were wounded in battle. The hymns sung to him in gratitude gave English the word for any outburst of praise.

why: His luxurious railway sleeping cars set the standard for comfortable long-distance travel.
story: Pullman built a whole company town for his workers, then cut wages without cutting rents. The strike that followed in 1894 shut down railways nationwide. He was buried under concrete to stop anyone digging him up.

why: He patented a light two-wheeled cab with the driver seated behind and above the passengers.
story: Hansom was an architect who designed a cab as a sideline, sold the patent for £10,000 and was never paid. The cab made London's streets fast; he went back to designing churches.

why: He commissioned a small enclosed carriage that could turn in a narrow street.
story: Brougham was a lawyer, a Lord Chancellor and a campaigner against slavery, and he is remembered for a carriage. He also popularised Cannes as a resort, more or less by accident, after being stranded there.

why: A four-wheeled carriage with a folding two-part roof was first built there.
mean: A carriage with a folding hood
story: The landau's roof splits in the middle and folds both ways, so passengers could be seen in fine weather and covered in bad. British royal processions still use them for exactly that reason.

who: Son of the sun god in Greek myth
why: He begged to drive the sun chariot, lost control, and scorched the earth.
mean: A light open carriage; a reckless driver
story: Phaethon took the reins of the sun for one day and nearly destroyed the world before Zeus shot him down. Naming a fast, unstable, open carriage after him was a joke that everyone at the time understood.

why: Edward VII took to wearing the local stiff felt hat and made it fashionable in Britain.
mean: A stiff felt hat with a curled brim
story: The future Edward VII visited the spa, liked the hat, and brought it home. Churchill wore one, and so did nearly every diplomat photographed between the wars.

who: Title character of George du Maurier's 1894 novel
why: The hat worn in the London stage version took the character's name.
mean: A soft felt hat with an indented crown
story: The novel that gave us the word Svengali also gave us the trilby — named not for the villain but for the heroine, from the hat worn onstage in the first London production.

why: They built a hard domed hat to protect gamekeepers' heads from low branches.
mean: A hard felt hat with a rounded crown
story: It was commissioned to stop gamekeepers being knocked off their horses by branches. The customer tested the prototype by putting it on the floor and stamping on it. It held, and he paid twelve shillings.

why: He knocked a tension spring off a shelf and watched it walk itself down.
mean: A coiled spring toy that walks downstairs
story: James was designing springs to steady instruments on rough seas when he knocked one off a shelf and watched it step end over end to the floor. His wife found the word slinky in a dictionary.

why: He built the cube to teach students about three-dimensional movement.
story: Rubik built it as a teaching aid and only realised he had made a puzzle when he scrambled it and could not put it back. It took him a month to solve his own invention.

why: The founder built the company name from the two Danish words.
story: Lego is short for leg godt, Danish for play well. By coincidence it also means I put together in Latin, which the company only discovered later and has been enjoying ever since.

why: The chef Escoffier created a peach dessert and a thin dry toast in her honour.
mean: Of dishes named for the singer: peach Melba, Melba toast
story: Escoffier served peach Melba in a swan carved from ice. The toast came later, when the singer was ill and could only manage something very thin and very dry. She got a dessert and a diet food.

why: He ordered the combination as a hangover cure at the Waldorf in 1894 and the chef put it on the menu.
mean: Poached eggs and ham on muffin with hollandaise
story: Benedict wandered into the Waldorf with a hangover and asked for buttered toast, bacon, poached eggs and hollandaise. The maitre d' was impressed enough to add it to the menu, swapping in muffin and ham.

why: A Venice barman named his peach-and-prosecco drink after a shade of pink in one of the painter's works.
mean: A cocktail of peach purée and prosecco
story: Giuseppe Cipriani mixed white peach purée with prosecco at Harry's Bar and thought the colour matched a saint's toga in a Bellini painting. A fifteenth-century artist therefore named a twentieth-century drink.

why: He asked a Florence barman to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda with gin.
mean: A cocktail of gin, vermouth and Campari
story: The count had reportedly spent time in America as a rodeo rider and came back wanting something stronger than the drink named after his adopted country. The barman swapped soda for gin, and added an orange slice to mark the difference.

why: A British biscuit maker named a currant-filled biscuit after him following his 1854 visit.
mean: A biscuit with a layer of currants
story: Garibaldi unified Italy and was mobbed by crowds on a visit to England. Britain honoured the liberator of a nation by naming a flat currant biscuit after him, universally known in playgrounds as squashed-fly.

why: His chef is credited with the thick centre-cut steak served with a reduction sauce.
mean: A thick cut of beef tenderloin
story: Chateaubriand was a novelist, ambassador and foreign minister, and is now mostly a steak. His cook grilled the fillet between two lesser cuts so the outer meat burned and the middle stayed perfect, then threw the outer pieces away.

why: The cheese-enriched white sauce is traditionally credited to him or to his household.
mean: A béchamel sauce enriched with cheese
story: Mornay was a Huguenot leader nicknamed the Pope of the Protestants, who spent his life on theological argument. The attribution of the sauce is shaky, which puts it in good company among French sauces.

why: A city ordinance of 1390 set standards for its mustard, and the recipe using verjuice was developed there.
story: Dijon mustard is a recipe, not a place of origin — the name is not protected, so most of it is made elsewhere. The seeds mostly come from Canada, which would surprise a fourteenth-century Burgundian.

why: The hard alpine cheese has been made in the district since at least the twelfth century.
story: Gruyere famously has no holes, despite being the cheese most cartoons draw with them. The holes belong to Emmental, which comes from a different Swiss valley entirely.

who: Valley of the river Emme in Switzerland
why: The cheese with large holes was made in the valley's dairies.
mean: A Swiss cheese with large holes
story: The holes are bubbles of carbon dioxide from bacteria, and dairies can control their size by adjusting the temperature. For years the holes got smaller because the milk got cleaner — fewer hay particles for bubbles to form around.

why: The soft white-rinded cheese has been made in the region since at least the eighth century.
mean: A soft cheese with a white rind
story: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with Europe being carved up, the delegates held a competition to name the finest cheese. Brie won, and was dubbed the king of cheeses — the only crown that congress awarded.

why: The blue cheese was traditionally made and aged in the town.
story: Legend says a distracted cheesemaker left curd overnight to chase a girl, added fresh curd in the morning to hide the lapse, and invented a blue cheese. Every blue cheese has a version of this story.

why: Any Italian cheese made from sheep's milk carries the name.
story: Not a place or a person — pecorino just means sheepish, in the literal sense. Roman legionaries were issued a daily ration of it, which makes it one of the oldest recorded packed lunches.

why: The cheese is made by cutting the stretched curd into pieces by hand.
story: Mozzarella is named after the action that makes it: the curd is heated, stretched like dough, and pinched off in lumps. The name means the cutting-off, which is exactly what the cheesemaker's hands are doing.

why: The new republic named itself after the man who led its liberation from Spain.
story: Bolivia is one of very few countries named after a real person. Bolivar liberated six nations and died poor and disillusioned, writing that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.

why: The republic took a Latinised form of his name at independence.
story: Columbus never set foot in Colombia. The name was chosen by a revolutionary who wanted a title for the whole of Spanish America, and it ended up attached to one country.

why: A Spanish explorer named the islands after the then crown prince.
story: Named in 1543 for a Spanish prince who never visited. There have been serious proposals to change it since independence, on the grounds that the country is named after a foreign monarch who colonised it.

why: He was the first European to reach the island, and it was renamed in his honour in 1856.
story: Tasman called it Van Diemen's Land after his sponsor. The name was changed in 1856 partly to shake off its association with convict transportation — so the island is named after the navigator instead of the governor.

why: The islands were claimed for France and named after the minister of the day.
mean: Island nation in the Indian Ocean
story: A hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean are named after a French finance minister who never saw them. He was in office for two years and is remembered nowhere else.

why: A German mapmaker labelled the new continent with the Latin form of his first name.
story: Martin Waldseemuller printed the name on a map in 1507 because Vespucci had argued it was a new continent rather than Asia. He later changed his mind and removed it — but a thousand copies were already out.

why: Romans named the islands for their large dogs; the bird was named after the islands.
story: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands are named after dogs — canis in Latin. So a small yellow songbird is, at two removes, named after a pack of large dogs.

why: English confused the American bird with a guinea fowl imported through Turkish merchants.
story: The bird is American and the name is a mistake. English traders met a similar African bird sold by Turkish merchants and called it turkey; when the American bird arrived it inherited the wrong name. The Turkish for it is hindi, meaning Indian.

why: His notation and results run through almost every branch of mathematics.
story: Euler gave us the symbols e, i, f(x) and the sigma for sums. He also wrote the equation many mathematicians call the most beautiful there is, tying together five fundamental constants in seven characters.

why: He studied processes where the next step depends only on the current state, not the history.
mean: Of a process with no memory of its past
story: Markov developed his chains partly to win an argument, analysing the vowels and consonants in a Pushkin poem to prove a rival wrong about probability. The maths now runs speech recognition and page ranking.

why: He coined the word fractal and found the set that carries his name.
story: Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and answered: it depends on the length of your ruler. Measure in smaller steps and it gets longer without limit. That question opened up fractal geometry.

why: His reformulation of mechanics underpins quantum theory.
story: Hamilton solved a problem he had wrestled with for years while walking along a Dublin canal, and carved the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge with a penknife. A plaque marks the spot; mathematicians still visit.

why: Groups where order does not matter are named in his honour.
mean: Of a group where the order of operations does not matter
story: Abel proved that no formula can solve every fifth-degree equation, settling a question three centuries old. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-six, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship.

why: The unit measures the biological effect of radiation, not merely the energy absorbed.
mean: The SI unit of radiation dose equivalent
story: A gray measures energy absorbed; a sievert measures how much harm it does, which depends on the kind of radiation. The difference matters: the same energy from alpha particles is twenty times more damaging.

why: He noticed a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire, linking electricity and magnetism.
mean: A unit of magnetic field strength
story: Orsted spotted it during a lecture, in front of students, when a compass on the bench moved as he switched on a current. He said nothing at the time and spent three months checking before publishing.

why: He invented the barometer and proved that air has weight.
mean: A unit of pressure, one millimetre of mercury
story: Torricelli filled a tube with mercury, upended it in a dish, and found the column always fell to about the same height — leaving a vacuum above it. Philosophers had insisted for two thousand years that a vacuum was impossible.

who: Disputed — probably a rowdy London family of Irish origin in the 1890s
why: Police reports and music-hall songs of the period attached the name to street disorder.
story: The word appears suddenly in London newspapers in the summer of 1898, already meaning street rowdy. Whether the Houlihans were a real family, a music-hall joke, or both, nobody has ever settled.

why: Textile workers destroying machinery in 1811 signed their threats as followers of General Ludd.
story: The Luddites were not against machines in principle — they were skilled workers whose trade was being destroyed and who had no vote to object with. Ned Ludd, in whose name they wrote, probably never existed.

who: German nobleman (1720-1797) whose tall tales were published as fiction
why: The real baron's exaggerated stories inspired a book of impossible adventures.
mean: Of wildly exaggerated tales; a disorder involving feigned illness
story: The real baron told entertaining war stories. A writer published a wildly embroidered version without asking, making him a laughing stock across Europe — he spent his last years trying to sue, and hated the book.

why: The drink is generally held to be named for the queen whose reign saw Protestant executions.
mean: A cocktail of vodka and tomato juice
story: The naming is disputed — rival theories point to a Chicago bar and a Hollywood actress. The queen's own nickname is not disputed: roughly 280 people were burned during her five-year reign.

who: Village and beach in eastern Cuba
why: An American engineer working at the nearby iron mines mixed rum, lime and sugar and named it for the place.
mean: A rum, lime and sugar cocktail
story: Jennings Cox ran out of gin while entertaining guests near the Daiquiri mines and improvised with local rum. Hemingway later drank them in Havana by the dozen, and had a variant named after him in turn.

who: Island borough of New York City
why: The cocktail is credited to a Manhattan club in the 1870s.
mean: A cocktail of whiskey and vermouth
story: The island's own name comes from a Lenape word usually translated as place where we get bows, after the wood that grew there. So the drink is named after an island named after a bow-making forest.

who: Spanish for 'daisy' — and a common given name
why: Several women named Margarita are claimed as the origin; the drink is also a member of the daisy family of cocktails.
mean: A tequila, lime and orange-liqueur cocktail
story: At least six people have claimed to have invented it for a woman named Margarita. The likelier answer is dull: daisy was already a category of cocktail, and margarita is simply the Spanish for daisy.

who: English surveyor who patented tarmacadam in 1902
why: He saw a barrel of tar spilled on a road, covered with slag, and set hard — and patented the process.
story: Hooley noticed a stretch of road outside an ironworks that was smooth and dustless, and learned a tar barrel had burst there and been covered with slag. He patented the accident and named it after McAdam.

why: Frederick Walton made the floor covering from oxidised linseed oil, and built the name from Latin.
story: Walton got the idea from the rubbery skin that forms on a tin of old paint. He never trademarked the name, and a court ruled in 1878 that it had already become generic — the first product ever to lose a name that way.

why: He forced through a law requiring a load line on ships' hulls to stop dangerous overloading.
mean: A ship's load line; a rubber-soled canvas shoe
story: Plimsoll campaigned against coffin ships — overloaded and over-insured vessels worth more sunk than afloat. The shoe is named after the line too: the rubber band round the sole looks just like a ship's load mark.

why: He developed the oral polio vaccine given on a sugar cube.
story: Sabin's vaccine could be swallowed rather than injected, which made mass campaigns possible in places with few doctors. Like Salk, he refused to patent it. The two men disliked each other for decades.

why: Hostages in a 1973 bank siege there defended their captors afterwards.
mean: Hostages developing sympathy for their captors
story: After six days in a bank vault, the hostages refused to testify against the robbers and some raised money for their defence. The psychiatrist who coined the term was himself part of the police negotiation.

why: His firm made the theatre organs and jukeboxes that carried the name into everyday speech.
story: Wurlitzer organs were built to replace whole orchestras in silent-film theatres — one player, hundreds of pipes, plus drums, cymbals, birdsong and a car horn. Sound film arrived and the market vanished almost overnight.

why: He carved mandolin and guitar tops like violin tops, and the company kept his name.
story: Gibson had no formal training and carved instrument tops from a single piece of wood, arched like a violin, when everyone else bent flat sheets. He sold the patent and the company outgrew him entirely.

why: He designed the first mass-produced solid-body electric guitar and bass.
story: Fender never learned to play the guitar. He was a radio repairman who approached the instrument as an engineering problem — bolt the neck on so it can be replaced, and the whole thing can be built on a production line.

why: He was rarely filmed without a cigarette, and the slang came from his habit of letting it hang from his lip.
mean: To keep something to oneself instead of sharing
story: To bogart something is to hog it, from the way Bogart kept a cigarette clamped in his mouth without ever seeming to smoke it. The word entered wide use through a 1968 song.

why: He and his son collected plants worldwide for English gardens.
mean: A trailing houseplant with striped leaves
story: The Tradescants kept a museum of curiosities in Lambeth called the Ark, open to anyone who paid sixpence — the first public museum in England. Its collection became the founding core of Oxford's Ashmolean.

why: Linnaeus named the genus after his patron and predecessor at Uppsala.
mean: A yellow daisy-like flower, the black-eyed Susan
story: Rudbeck discovered the lymphatic system as a student, and later spent decades trying to prove that Sweden was the lost Atlantis. Linnaeus named the flower for him regardless.

why: Two botanists found the tree in Georgia and named it for their friend.
mean: A flowering tree, extinct in the wild
story: The Bartrams found this tree growing in one small patch in Georgia in 1765 and collected seeds. It has not been seen in the wild since 1803. Every franklinia alive today descends from those seeds.

why: The genus was named for the head gardener of the Vienna palace gardens.
story: Its other name is dumb cane: the sap contains needle-shaped crystals that make the mouth and throat swell, temporarily robbing anyone who chews it of speech. It remains a popular office plant.

why: The genus was named for the emperor's physician, who was also a botanist.
mean: A shade plant grown for its leaves
story: Hostas are grown for foliage rather than flowers, thrive in shade, and are eaten enthusiastically by slugs. Host himself was physician to the Austrian emperor and ran the imperial botanical garden.

who: English word meaning to scratch or grope about
why: The inventor renamed his word game, which had failed under two earlier names.
story: Alfred Butts, an out-of-work architect, counted letter frequencies on the front page of the New York Times to set the tile values. The game failed twice under other names before Scrabble stuck.

why: The inventor grew up in Ghana and took the name from Swahili.
story: Leslie Scott's family played it with wooden blocks from a sawmill in Ghana. She named it from the Swahili kujenga, to build — which is slightly ironic for a game everyone plays in order to watch it fall over.

who: Economic term for exclusive control of a market
why: The game was adapted from The Landlord's Game, designed to demonstrate the harm monopolies cause.
story: Elizabeth Magie invented the original in 1904 as a protest against landlords hoarding property. Decades later a man sold a version to Parker Brothers as his own invention. She was paid five hundred dollars.

why: He composed the marches that defined American band music and asked for a tuba to be redesigned for marching.
story: Sousa wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever, the official national march of the United States. He also campaigned against recorded music, warning it would stop people learning instruments — a prediction with some merit.

why: His Alessandria workshop became the most famous felt hat maker in the world.
story: A Borsalino takes around seven weeks and dozens of separate operations to make, mostly from rabbit felt. The firm was still going after more than 160 years, which very few hat companies can say.

why: An American doctor named his antiseptic after the pioneer of antiseptic surgery.
story: Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic, then as a floor cleaner and a cure for gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash when the makers popularised the word halitosis to convince people they had a problem.

why: Ships out of the port carried a minced beef dish that took the city's name.
mean: A patty of minced beef served in a bun
story: Sailors leaving one busy German port ate a minced beef steak served flat on a plate. They carried the habit across the Atlantic, cooks there slid the patty into a bun, and the sandwich kept the port city's name.

who: an American president and keen hunter (1858-1919)
why: He refused to shoot a tethered bear, and a cartoon of the moment inspired a toymaker.
story: On a hunting trip a president refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree, calling it unsporting. A newspaper cartoon spread the story, a shopkeeper sewed a plush bear in tribute, and the toy carried his nickname ever after.

why: The handling game grew up in that school's playing fields and took its name.
mean: A team sport played with an oval ball that players may carry
story: At one English school the football rules allowed a player to pick the ball up and run with it. Old boys carried the handling version to clubs everywhere, and to tell it apart from the kicking game people simply called it by the school's name.

who: a coastal region on the Adriatic
why: The spotted coach dog was associated with that coast and named for it.
mean: A white dog covered in black or brown spots
story: A tall spotted dog that loved to trot beside horses became fashionable as a carriage escort. Early writers linked the breed to one stretch of Adriatic coastline, and although the connection is thin, the region's name stuck to the dog for good.

who: a rugged region of eastern Canada
why: The water dog came from the coast of that region.
mean: A strong, friendly retriever with a short water-shedding coat
story: Fishermen on a cold Canadian coast kept short-haired dogs that dived into freezing water after nets and fish. English gentlemen brought the dogs home, bred them for the shooting field, and named them after the coast they came from.

why: The tiny dog was first noticed by travellers in that state.
mean: A very small dog with large upright ears
story: American visitors to a northern Mexican state in the 1800s bought tiny dogs from villagers near the border. Nobody recorded a breed name, so the buyers simply used the name of the state, and the smallest dog in the world has answered to it since.

who: the ancient empire of modern Iran
why: Romans thought the fruit came from there and called it the Persian apple.
mean: A soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large stone
story: The fruit really began in China, but it reached Rome along the road from Persia. Roman growers called it the Persian apple, persicum, and centuries of shortening in French wore that long name down to a single soft syllable.

why: The wild coffee plant grows there, and the drink's name traces back through Arabic to it.
mean: A hot drink brewed from roasted ground beans
story: Wild bushes with red berries still grow in one Ethiopian highland. Traders carried the beans to Arabia, where the brewed drink became qahwa, and every European name for it -- cafe, kaffee and the English word -- goes back to that first green hillside.

who: the Greek titan of the world-encircling river
why: Greeks pictured a vast river running round the edge of the earth and named it after him.
mean: A very large expanse of salt water
story: Greeks imagined the earth as a flat disc ringed by one endless river, and gave that river the name of a titan, the eldest son of sky and earth. When sailors learned the water went on much further than they thought, the titan's name went with it.

who: sea creatures in Greek myth whose singing lured sailors onto rocks
why: A warning device that wails was named after the singers whose voices meant danger.
mean: A device that makes a loud wailing warning sound
story: In the old story, singers on a rocky island sang so beautifully that crews steered towards them and were wrecked. Odysseus tied himself to the mast to hear them safely. Centuries later an inventor gave the name to a machine whose wail means danger.

who: the ash-covered heroine of a fairy tale retold by Charles Perrault
why: Her sudden rise from drudgery to glory became the name for any such transformation.
mean: Someone overlooked who suddenly rises to success
story: A girl who slept beside the fireplace and was named for the cinders in her clothes went to the ball and left one slipper behind. Now any unfancied team that reaches the final, or any ignored talent that shines, gets called by her name.

who: the girl in the tale of the three bears
why: Her habit of rejecting extremes and choosing the middle option became a scientific shorthand.
mean: Neither too much nor too little; just right
story: A girl in a fairy tale tried porridge too hot, then too cold, then just right. Astronomers borrowed her fussiness: a planet in the narrow band that is neither too hot nor too cold for water now sits in the zone named for her.

who: the boy who would not grow up, created by J. M. Barrie
why: His refusal to age became the name for adults who never quite do either.
mean: An adult who refuses to grow up
story: A playwright invented a boy who flew, fought pirates, and flatly refused to get any older. Psychologists later borrowed him: someone who dodges every adult responsibility and stays a delighted child is said to have his syndrome.

who: the tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
why: His riddles and wild manner made his name a byword for cheerful nonsense.
mean: A person who behaves in a wildly eccentric way
story: At a tea party that never ended, a hat-maker asked a riddle he could not answer and poured tea on a dormouse. Real hat-makers of the day were poisoned by the mercury they used, which is why madness and hat-making went together in the joke.

who: the grinning cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
why: It faded away leaving only its grin, so its name attaches to any wide fixed smile.
story: A cat in a wonderland book sat in a tree, gave unhelpful directions, and vanished slowly from the tail forwards until nothing was left but its grin. Anyone smiling that widely for no clear reason is now said to be grinning like it.

who: the egg who sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme
why: Because he could not be put back together, his name means anything broken beyond repair.
mean: Something so broken it cannot be mended
story: An egg sat on a wall, fell off, and all the king's horses and men could do nothing about it. Writers now reach for his name whenever a treaty, a company or a friendship has shattered in a way no committee is going to fix.

who: a small town in eastern Belgium
why: Its iron-rich springs drew visitors from all over Europe, and the town's name became the word for any such resort.
mean: A resort with mineral springs or health treatments
story: A Belgian town with bubbling iron-rich springs became the fashionable place to take the waters in the 1500s. Visitors came home saying they had been to the town by name, and soon every mineral bath in Europe was borrowing it.

why: The little fish were caught in huge numbers off its coast.
mean: A small oily fish often packed tightly in tins
story: Fishing boats around one large Mediterranean island hauled in silver shoals of a small oily fish by the tonne. The catch was salted, shipped and eventually tinned, and it carried the island's name to breakfast tables everywhere.

who: a stately home in Gloucestershire, England
why: Guests of the duke played the shuttlecock game in its great hall.
mean: A racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net
story: Officers home from India brought back a shuttlecock game and played it in the hall of an English duke's country house on a wet afternoon. When people asked what the game was called, they answered with the name of the house.

why: He built the giant rotating wheel for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.
mean: A giant upright rotating wheel with passenger cars
story: Chicago wanted something to outdo the Eiffel Tower. A bridge engineer proposed a wheel two hundred and fifty feet across, carrying two thousand people at once. Everyone said it would collapse; it did not, and every big wheel since has borne his name.

who: the land the stone was traded through
why: The blue-green stone reached Europe by Turkish traders, so French called it the Turkish stone.
mean: A blue-green mineral, or that colour
story: The blue-green stone was mined in Persia, but it reached Venice and Paris in the packs of Turkish merchants. French buyers called it pierre turquoise, the Turkish stone, and the shortened word now names the colour as much as the mineral.

who: a town in the Mexican state of Jalisco
why: The blue agave spirit is distilled in and around it.
mean: A Mexican spirit distilled from blue agave
story: In the red volcanic soil around one Mexican town, blue agave plants grow for years before their hearts are roasted and distilled. Mexican law now says the spirit may only carry the town's name if it comes from that region.

who: a historic region on the Baltic coast
why: The tiny fluffy dog was bred down from larger sled dogs of that region.
mean: A very small long-haired dog with a plumed tail
story: Big white spitz dogs pulled sleds along a cold Baltic coast. Breeders shrank them generation by generation until Queen Victoria fell for an eleven-pound one and made the miniature fashionable, and the region's name shrank onto the little dog.

why: Butchers there used the powerful dogs to drive cattle and guard money.
mean: A large powerful black-and-tan guard dog
story: Butchers in a German market town used heavy dogs to drive cattle to market, then tied the purse of takings round the dog's neck for the walk home. Nobody robbed them. The town's name went onto the breed and stayed.

why: The pale cat with dark points was first brought to the West from the Siamese royal court.
mean: A slender pale cat with dark face, ears, paws and tail
story: A pair of pale blue-eyed cats with sooty faces was given to a British consul by a royal court in South East Asia in 1884. They were shown in London the next year, astonished everybody, and took the kingdom's old name as their own.

who: a stretch of West African coast
why: The South American rodent reached Europe on ships from that trade route and picked up the wrong continent's name.
mean: A small tailless rodent kept as a pet or used in experiments
story: The animal is not a pig and has never been near West Africa: it comes from the Andes. But it arrived in Europe aboard ships working the Guinea trade route, sailors named it after the last coast they had seen, and the mistake stuck.

who: a port on the Red Sea coast of Yemen
why: The world's coffee once shipped from that harbour.
mean: A rich coffee, or coffee flavoured with chocolate
story: For two hundred years almost every coffee bean that reached Europe left through one Yemeni harbour. The beans had a chocolatey edge, so when cooks later stirred cocoa into coffee they reached for the harbour's name to describe it.

why: Dutch plantations there supplied so much coffee that the island's name became slang for the drink.
story: Dutch growers planted coffee across one Indonesian island until it supplied much of the world. American sailors and soldiers took to calling any cup of coffee by the island's name, and a programming language later borrowed it as a nod to the coders' fuel.

why: The bean was exported from that port in boxes stamped with the city's name.
story: Crates of a broad flat bean left a Peruvian port stamped with the city of origin. Buyers in North America read the stamp rather than any botanical label, and started ordering the beans by the name of the city instead.

why: A chance seedling on her farm produced the hard green apple.
mean: A hard, tart, bright green apple
story: An Australian orchardist threw some French crab apple cores onto a creek bank. A seedling came up, and its fruit turned out hard, sharp and green, and kept for months. Neighbours called it by her nickname and the apple never lost it.

why: A botanist friend named the Australian nut tree in his honour.
mean: A hard-shelled Australian nut with rich creamy flesh
story: A botanist studying rainforest trees in Queensland found one with a nut so hard you needed a hammer. He named the genus after a chemist friend who, as it happens, never tasted the nut that would carry his name around the world.

why: He is credited with building the grilled corned-beef sandwich during a weekly poker game.
mean: A grilled sandwich of corned beef, sauerkraut, cheese and dressing on rye
story: A grocer playing his weekly poker game in an Omaha hotel asked the kitchen for corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and dressing between rye bread, grilled. The hotel owner put it on the menu under the player's first name, and it never came off.

why: The layered pastry's French name, napolitain, drifted into the emperor's name in English.
mean: A layered pastry of puff pastry and cream
story: The layered cream slice began as a Naples pastry, napolitain in French. English speakers heard the more famous name in it and rewrote the word, so the dessert now honours an emperor who had nothing whatever to do with inventing it.

who: a city in northern Italy famous for its cooking
why: The slow-cooked meat sauce is the city's signature dish.
mean: A slow-cooked Italian meat and tomato sauce
story: Cooks in one wealthy northern Italian city simmered minced meat with a little tomato, milk and wine for hours, and served it with wide flat pasta. The city's name travelled with the recipe, though what most countries make of it would horrify the locals.

why: Ice cream sellers from the city introduced the three-flavour brick abroad.
mean: Ice cream in three coloured layers
story: Ice cream makers from a southern Italian port emigrated in the 1800s and sold moulded ice cream in coloured stripes, in imitation of their national flag. Abroad the layers became chocolate, vanilla and strawberry, and kept the city's name.

who: a port city in south-west France
why: The red wine of the surrounding vineyards is shipped from and named for it.
mean: A red wine from the region around one French port
story: For centuries English merchants bought red wine at one French Atlantic port and shipped it home in barrels. They called it by the harbour rather than the vineyard, and even now the region's most famous wines answer to the port's name.

who: the country the dye was traded from
why: Greeks called the deep blue dye the Indian substance.
mean: A deep blue-violet dye or colour
story: Greek traders met a deep blue dye that came in hard cakes from the East, and called it indikon, simply the Indian thing. The name outlasted the trade: the colour between blue and violet in the rainbow still carries the country's name.

who: the Mediterranean island whose mines supplied Rome
why: Romans called the metal aes cyprium, the metal of Cyprus.
mean: A soft reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity well
story: Rome got most of its reddish metal from mines on one Mediterranean island, and called it the Cyprus metal. Latin wore aes cyprium down to cuprum, and English wore that down again, so an island's name now sits in every electrical cable.

who: a border region between France and Germany
why: British breeders renamed the German shepherd after the region during the First World War.
story: During the First World War British owners could not bring themselves to call the breed a German shepherd. They renamed it after a border region that had changed hands between the two countries, and in Britain the wartime alias lasted for decades.

who: the old English name for Beijing
why: The flat-faced dogs were bred in the Chinese imperial palace and taken from it in 1860.
mean: A small flat-faced dog with a long flowing coat
story: Only the Chinese imperial family could keep the little lion dogs of the palace. When British and French troops looted the Summer Palace in 1860 five were carried off, one was given to Queen Victoria, and the capital's old name went with them.

who: the peninsula where the breed was developed
why: Bedouin tribes bred the horse for endurance in the desert.
mean: A horse breed with a dished face, high tail and great stamina
story: Desert tribes bred horses that could go far on little water and live close to the family tent. The line is one of the oldest kept anywhere, and almost every modern racing breed carries some of its blood along with the peninsula's name.

who: the many-headed water serpent of Greek myth
why: Cutting off one head grew two, so any problem that multiplies when attacked takes its name.
mean: A problem that grows worse each time you attack it
story: Heracles found that every head he sliced off the marsh serpent was replaced by two more, and only fire could stop the regrowth. Ever since, a difficulty that spawns two new difficulties each time you solve it has been called by the monster's name.

who: the great serpent of Delphi killed by Apollo
why: Naturalists borrowed the myth-serpent's name for the huge constricting snakes.
mean: A large snake that kills by constriction
story: A monstrous serpent guarded the spring at Delphi until Apollo shot it, and the oracle's priestess took her title from it. When naturalists needed a name for enormous constricting snakes, they reached back into the myth for the serpent's own.

who: the Roman goddess of the dawn
why: The glowing polar lights were named for the goddess who coloured the morning sky.
mean: The coloured lights that glow in polar skies
story: Romans said a goddess rose each morning to paint the eastern sky before the sun came up. When Galileo needed a name for the green and red curtains that hang over the far north, he gave them hers, adding the northern dawn.

who: the Roman goddess and personification of the moon
why: Madness was believed to come and go with the phases of the moon.
mean: A person behaving wildly or foolishly
story: Doctors from Rome to the Middle Ages believed that fits of madness rose and fell with the phases of the moon, and English law once separated the permanently ill from those thought to change with it. The moon goddess's name is still inside the word.

who: the unseen ruler in George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: His name became shorthand for a state that watches everything its citizens do.
story: In a novel published in 1949 every wall carried a poster of a moustached face and the line that he was watching you. Nobody in the book ever meets him. Seventy years on, his name is the fastest way to say a state is watching too closely.

who: a county in Kentucky named for a French royal house
why: Corn whiskey barrelled and shipped from that county took its name.
mean: American whiskey distilled mainly from corn and aged in charred oak
story: Barrels of corn whiskey floated down the Ohio and Mississippi from one Kentucky county, whose name was stencilled on the staves. By the time they reached New Orleans the oak had mellowed the spirit, and buyers asked for it by the county on the barrel.

why: The thick woollen cloth used for the bags was woven there.
mean: A cylindrical canvas bag closed with a drawstring
story: A Belgian town wove a thick coarse wool that soldiers and sailors trusted to keep out weather. Coats and kitbags cut from it carried the town's name across every navy in Europe, and the bag kept the name long after the cloth changed.

who: an American ice-rink owner and inventor (1901-1988)
why: He built the first machine that resurfaces an ice rink in one pass.
mean: A machine that shaves and resurfaces ice
story: Resurfacing a rink took five men over an hour. A rink owner in California spent nine years bolting a shaving blade, a water tank and a squeegee onto an army surplus chassis until one driver could do it in ten minutes. His name is now on the machine everywhere.

who: the daughter of an Austrian car dealer (1889-1929)
why: Her father entered cars under her name, and the maker adopted it.
story: An Austrian businessman raced Daimler cars under his young daughter's name because a foreign entrant needed a pseudonym. The cars won, dealers demanded that model by that name, and the factory quietly made a ten-year-old girl's name its own.

who: the French officer who founded Detroit in 1701
why: The Detroit carmaker took the city founder's name and coat of arms.
mean: An American luxury car; anything of the highest quality
story: A French officer built a fort on a narrow strait and called it the place of the strait, which became Detroit. Two centuries later a carmaker in that city borrowed his name and his family crest, and the word came to mean the best of anything.

who: a Swiss racing driver and engineer (1878-1941)
why: He co-founded the car company that carries his surname.
story: A Swiss racing driver went into partnership with an ousted car executive, lending his famous name to a new company. He fell out with his partner over building cheap cars, sold his shares early, and watched his surname become one of the biggest in America.

who: an American frontiersman who died at the Alamo (1796-1836)
why: His fighting knife became famous after a sandbar brawl in 1827.
mean: A large single-edged sheath knife with a clipped point
story: A frontiersman was shot and stabbed in a duel-turned-brawl on a Mississippi sandbar and still killed two men with a heavy butcher's knife. Newspapers described the blade in detail, smiths were flooded with orders, and the knife took his name.

who: a fortified city in south-west France
why: The blade that fits a musket muzzle was first made or first used there.
mean: A blade fixed to the muzzle of a rifle
story: The story goes that soldiers besieged in a French border city ran out of powder and jammed their hunting knives into their musket barrels. Whether or not that happened, the city's forges made the blades, and its name went onto them.

why: European makers copied Japanese lacquerwork and called the hard glossy black finish by the country's name.
mean: A hard glossy black lacquer finish
story: Lacquered boxes arriving from East Asia in the 1600s astonished Europe with a black finish nothing local could match. Workshops in England and France tried to copy it, sold the results as the country's own name, and turned a nation into a verb.

why: The island's fishermen wore a close-knit woollen jumper that took its name.
mean: A close-fitting knitted woollen jumper; also a breed of dairy cow
story: Fishermen on a small Channel Island knitted jumpers so tightly that seawater ran off them. Naval crews adopted the pattern, Australian footballers borrowed the word for their shirts, and the island's dairy cattle carried the same name to farms worldwide.

why: The heavy draught horse was bred by farmers along that valley.
mean: A very large draught horse with feathered legs
story: Farmers in one Scottish river valley crossed local mares with imported Flemish stallions to get a horse that could haul coal and plough heavy clay. The breed grew to a tonne, kept its white feathered legs, and carried the valley's name to the world.

why: The tiny dried grapes were shipped from there as raisins of Corinth.
mean: A small dried grape used in baking
story: Medieval traders bought tiny seedless dried grapes at a Greek port and sold them in England as raisins of that city. The phrase wore down over centuries until only a mangled version of the city's name was left on the packet.

who: an ancient port in the Levant, now Ashkelon
why: Crusaders brought the small clustered onion home and named it after the port.
mean: A small mild onion that grows in clusters
story: Returning crusaders brought back a small onion that grew in clusters and tasted milder than the ones at home. They said it came from one Levantine port, called it the onion of that place, and French cooks wore the phrase down to a single word.

who: a river in ancient Colchis, on the Black Sea
why: Greeks said the bird came from the banks of that river.
mean: A long-tailed game bird with bright plumage
story: Greek sailors returning from the Black Sea brought back a spectacular long-tailed bird and said it lived along one particular river. They called it the bird of the Phasis, and every European language still carries a worn-down version of that river's name.

who: the Italian word for sunflower, misheard as a city name
why: The plant is a sunflower relative, and girasole was corrupted into a holy city's name.
mean: A knobbly edible tuber from a sunflower relative
story: The knobbly tuber is a North American sunflower and has never grown near the Middle East. Italians called the plant girasole, turning to the sun; English ears heard a famous city in that word, and the wrong name has stuck for four hundred years.

why: The butter-and-egg sauce was said to imitate a Dutch style of cooking.
mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter and lemon
story: French cooks named several sauces after foreign countries to suggest a style rather than an origin. This one, whisked from yolks and warm butter until it thickens, was labelled Dutch, possibly because the Netherlands supplied the butter.

who: a region in the French Pyrenees
why: The sauce was named at a restaurant honouring a king born in that region.
mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter, tarragon and shallot
story: A chef outside Paris invented a herbed butter sauce at a restaurant named for Henry IV, who was born in a Pyrenean region and nicknamed for it. The sauce took the region's name, though nobody there had ever made it.

who: a hilly wine region in Tuscany
why: The red wine comes from vineyards in those hills.
story: A grand duke drew a boundary round some Tuscan hills in 1716 and declared that only wine from inside it could carry the region's name. It was one of the first protected wine areas anywhere, three centuries before such rules became normal.

who: a wine region north of Lyon in France
why: The light red wine made from gamay grapes there carries the region's name.
story: Growers in a French region north of Lyon make a light red from gamay grapes and release the newest vintage on the third Thursday of November. Bottles race to Paris and beyond overnight, and the region's name goes with every cork.

who: a village in the Maconnais, Burgundy
why: The white grape variety takes the village's name.
mean: A white wine grape, or the wine made from it
story: A small Burgundy village gave its name to a green-skinned grape that turned out to grow almost anywhere, from Champagne to California to Australia. It is now the most planted white wine grape on earth, still carrying one village's name.

who: a wine region in northern Spain
why: The oak-aged red wine of the Ebro valley takes the region's name.
mean: A Spanish red wine aged in oak
story: When disease wrecked French vineyards in the 1800s, Bordeaux winemakers crossed the Pyrenees and taught growers in a northern Spanish valley to age wine in oak barrels. The region kept the technique, and its name now means oak-aged Spanish red.

who: the Greek Muse of epic poetry
why: The steam whistle organ was named for the Muse whose name means beautiful-voiced.
mean: A loud musical instrument of steam whistles
story: An inventor in 1855 mounted a keyboard on a row of steam whistles loud enough to be heard eight miles away. He named it for the Muse of epic poetry, whose name means beautiful-voiced, which anyone who has stood near a circus one may dispute.

who: the brutish human-like creatures in Gulliver's Travels
why: Swift's filthy, violent creatures gave their name to any coarse lout.
story: On his last voyage Gulliver meets talking horses ruling over filthy, howling creatures that look uncomfortably like humans. Swift meant it as a mirror. The creatures' name became an insult, and much later a search engine picked it up as a joke.

who: the impossible rule in Joseph Heller's 1961 novel
why: The rule made escape logically impossible, so its name means any such trap.
mean: A problem whose only solution is blocked by the problem itself
story: A bomber pilot could be grounded for insanity, but asking to be grounded proved he was sane enough to fly. Heller's invented regulation was so exact a picture of bureaucratic traps that its number entered the dictionary within a decade.

who: the shrinking official language in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: Its purpose was to make rebellious thought impossible by deleting words.
mean: Deliberately ambiguous or misleading official language
story: In Orwell's novel the state shrinks the dictionary every year, on the theory that a thought you have no word for cannot be thought at all. The invented language's name is now used for any official wording designed to blur rather than explain.

who: the mental habit demanded by the Party in Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: It meant holding two contradictory beliefs at once and accepting both.
mean: Holding two contradictory beliefs at the same time
story: Orwell's Party required citizens to believe two opposite things at once and to be sincere about both, forgetting the contradiction and then forgetting the forgetting. The coined word escaped the novel and is now used of real politics every week.

who: the acrobatic trickster servant of Italian commedia dell'arte
why: His diamond-patterned costume gave the word for that pattern.
mean: A pattern of coloured diamonds; a comic acrobatic character
story: A masked servant character in Italian street comedy wore a patched costume that hardened over time into neat coloured diamonds. He tumbled, schemed and chased Columbine through two centuries of theatre, and left his name on the pattern itself.

who: the servant clowns of Italian commedia dell'arte
why: The clown who mimicked his master gave his name to anything absurdly comic.
story: In Italian street comedy the servant clowns, named from a dialect form of Giovanni, copied their masters' gestures badly on purpose. English audiences took the troupe's name for the behaviour, and it now describes any cheerfully absurd person.

why: The gas was detected in the sun's spectrum before it was found on earth.
mean: The lightest inert gas, used to fill balloons
story: During an eclipse in 1868 astronomers saw a yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched no known element. They named the unknown gas after the Greek sun god. Twenty-seven years passed before anyone found any of it on earth.

why: He imported the plum from France, and the labels were lost in transit.
story: An English baronet imported plum trees from a French monastery, and the labels were lost on the way. His gardener, needing something to call the green ones, combined the colour with his employer's surname, and the plum has answered to it since.

why: He distributed the English Williams pear in America under his own name.
story: An English variety called the Williams pear was already growing on a Massachusetts farm when a merchant bought the land. Not knowing the name, he propagated and sold it under his own. The same fruit still has two names on two sides of the Atlantic.

who: a Soviet tank sergeant turned weapons designer (1919-2013)
why: He designed the rifle while recovering from wounds in 1942.
story: A wounded Soviet tank sergeant lay in hospital listening to comrades complain that German troops had better automatic weapons. He sketched a design built to work when filled with mud or sand. Over a hundred million have been made, all carrying his name.

why: His bolt-action rifle became the pattern copied by most armies.
mean: A German bolt-action rifle or pistol
story: A German designer perfected a bolt action so reliable that armies from Spain to Japan bought or copied it, and hunting rifles still use his locking system a century later. His surname is stamped on more military rifles than almost any other.

why: He found that energy comes in fixed packets set by one small number.
mean: The fixed quantity linking a photon's energy to its frequency
story: A German physicist trying to explain the colour of hot glowing objects found the maths only worked if energy came in indivisible packets. He called the idea a desperate act. It founded quantum theory, and the tiny number in it carries his name.

why: He pictured electrons in fixed orbits that could only jump between set levels.
mean: A picture of the atom with electrons in fixed energy orbits
story: A Danish physicist proposed that electrons could only sit in certain orbits and jumped between them by swallowing or spitting out exact packets of light. It explained hydrogen's spectrum precisely, was wrong in detail, and is still the first atom every student draws.

why: He hung a heavy pendulum in the Pantheon to show the earth turning beneath it.
mean: A long free-swinging pendulum that demonstrates the earth's rotation
story: In 1851 a French physicist hung a sixty-seven-metre wire from the dome of the Pantheon with a heavy iron ball on the end. As it swung, its path slowly rotated. Paris could watch the planet turning for the first time, in a public hall.

why: He showed that fluid speeds up and its pressure drops in a narrowing pipe.
mean: The drop in pressure when a fluid speeds through a narrowing
story: An Italian priest and physicist showed that squeezing a pipe makes the fluid inside run faster and press outwards less. Carburettors, atomisers, aircraft instruments and hospital suction all use the trick, and all carry his name for it.

why: He found a single number that predicts whether flow will be smooth or turbulent.
mean: A number predicting whether a flow will be smooth or turbulent
story: An engineer injected a thread of dye into water flowing down a glass pipe. Below a certain speed the thread stayed straight; above it, the dye burst into swirls. He reduced the whole question to one dimensionless ratio that now bears his name.

why: He rated tornado strength by the damage left behind.
mean: A scale rating tornado strength by damage
story: A meteorologist who had surveyed the blast damage at Nagasaki applied the same eye to tornado wreckage, working backwards from broken buildings to wind speed. His damage-based scale, from a snapped branch to a house swept clean off its slab, still rates every twister.

why: He showed how to rebuild a function from its derivatives at a single point.
mean: An infinite sum that reproduces a function from its derivatives at one point
story: An English mathematician showed that if you know a curve's height, slope, curvature and every higher rate of change at just one point, you can rebuild the entire curve as an endless sum. Almost all of numerical computing rests on that trick.

why: He generalised ordinary geometry to spaces with infinitely many dimensions.
mean: A complete space with infinitely many dimensions and a notion of angle
story: A German mathematician extended ordinary distance and angle into spaces with endlessly many directions. It sounded like pure abstraction until quantum mechanics arrived and turned out to need exactly that geometry to describe the state of a particle.

why: He studied the matrix of partial derivatives that tells how a transformation stretches space.
mean: The matrix of partial derivatives of a vector function
story: A German mathematician studied the grid of partial derivatives that says how much a change of coordinates stretches or twists each direction. Its determinant is the factor by which volume changes, which is why it appears in every multiple integral.

why: He studied the square array of second derivatives that describes curvature.
mean: The square matrix of second partial derivatives of a function
story: A German mathematician assembled all the second derivatives of a function into one square array. Its signs tell you whether a flat point is a peak, a valley or a saddle, which is why every optimisation algorithm reaches for it.

who: a plateau town in the Veneto, northern Italy
why: The cow's-milk cheese has been made on that plateau for centuries.
story: Shepherds on a high plateau in northern Italy once made this cheese from sheep's milk. When cattle replaced the flocks the recipe changed but the name did not, and European law now protects it for that plateau alone.

why: A cheesemaker's son invented the washed-curd cheese there in 1885.
mean: A mild orange American cheese with a springy texture
story: A Wisconsin cheesemaker's teenage son washed the curds in cold water instead of letting them cook dry, and got a softer, milder, moister cheese than cheddar. It was the first cheese invented in America, and it took the little town's name.

why: A Danish cheesemaker developed the cheese at that farm in the 1800s.
mean: A semi-soft Danish cheese with small holes
story: A Danish woman toured European dairies, came home to an experimental farm outside Copenhagen, and worked out a semi-soft cheese full of tiny irregular holes. The farm's name went onto it, and Denmark's best-known cheese was born on a research plot.

why: The city's cooks breadcrumb and fry veal, and saffron their risotto.
mean: Coated in breadcrumbs and fried, in the style of one Italian city
story: A northern Italian city gave its name to two very different dishes: a veal cutlet beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried in butter, and a risotto turned gold with saffron. Vienna's schnitzel is very probably the same cutlet under another flag.

who: a French city famous for its cooking
why: Dishes finished with sliced onions are named for the city's style.
mean: Cooked with sliced onions, in the style of one French city
story: One French city is so serious about food that its small restaurants have their own name, bouchons. Any dish labelled with the city's adjective on a French menu comes with sliced onions browned in butter, whatever else is on the plate.

who: a sunny region of southern France
why: Dishes with tomato, garlic and olive oil take the region's name.
mean: Cooked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
story: The name of a southern French region on a menu promises the same three things every time: tomato, garlic and olive oil, usually with herbs from the dry hills. The region's Roman name simply meant the province, the first one Rome held outside Italy.

who: the miserly old Venetian merchant of commedia dell'arte
why: His tight leg-covering costume gave its name to trousers.
mean: Wide or tight trousers, depending on the century
story: A stock character in Italian street comedy played a mean old Venetian merchant in tight full-length hose, unusual when other men wore breeches. Audiences named the garment after him, French shortened it, and the word ended up as plain pants.

who: the boastful cowardly soldier of commedia dell'arte
why: His swagger and swift retreat made his name a word for a boastful rogue.
mean: A boastful coward; a roguish clown
story: A stock character in Italian comedy strutted in black with a sword, boasted of battles he had not fought, and ran at the first real threat. His name, from a word meaning skirmish, became the English word for exactly that sort of man.

who: the hypocritical architect in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit
why: He preached morality endlessly while behaving badly, so his name means smug hypocrisy.
story: Dickens created an architect who never designed a building, lived off his pupils' work, and lectured everyone he met about virtue while cheating them. His name became the exact English word for moralising that the moraliser has no intention of following.

why: He wrote the wave equation that governs how a quantum state evolves.
mean: The equation describing how a quantum wavefunction changes over time
story: An Austrian physicist on a winter holiday in the Alps wrote down a wave equation that predicted the hydrogen spectrum exactly. He later invented a thought experiment about a cat to show how absurd he found the standard reading of his own equation.

why: He showed that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
mean: The rule that position and momentum cannot both be measured precisely
story: A young German physicist working alone on Helgoland realised that the sharper you pin down where a particle is, the vaguer its momentum must become, and not because your instruments are poor. The limit is built into nature, and it carries his name.

why: He showed that no two electrons can share the same quantum state.
mean: The rule that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state
story: An Austrian physicist, famous for a scathing tongue and for equipment that broke when he entered the room, showed that two electrons can never sit in exactly the same state. That single refusal is why atoms have shells and why matter takes up space.

why: He found the constant that fixes the wavelengths of an atom's spectral lines.
mean: The constant setting the wavelengths of atomic spectral lines
story: A Swedish physicist hunting for pattern in the coloured lines of glowing gases found one formula that fitted them all, with a single number in it. He had no idea why it worked; Bohr's atom explained it thirty years later.

why: He linked the temperature of matter to the statistics of its moving particles.
mean: The constant relating temperature to the average energy of particles
story: An Austrian physicist argued that heat is just particles jostling and that entropy counts the ways they can be arranged. Colleagues mocked the idea for decades. His formula is carved on his gravestone, and the constant in it carries his name.

why: He built a set by repeatedly deleting middle thirds, and founded set theory.
mean: A set formed by repeatedly removing the middle third of an interval
story: A German mathematician took a line, cut out the middle third, cut the middle third from each remaining piece, and kept going forever. What is left has no length at all yet contains uncountably many points, which is the sort of thing that made his colleagues furious.

who: a French mathematician killed in a duel at twenty (1811-1832)
why: He linked the solvability of equations to the symmetry group of their roots.
mean: The theory linking equation solvability to the symmetry of the roots
story: A French student twice failed his entrance exams, was expelled for politics, and spent the night before a duel writing out his mathematics with a note in the margin saying he had no time. He died at twenty. The theory reshaped algebra.

why: He claimed a proof in a book margin and never wrote it down.
mean: The claim that no cube or higher power splits into two like powers
story: A French lawyer scribbled in the margin of a book that he had a proof but the margin was too small to hold it. Three and a half centuries and thousands of failed attempts later, Andrew Wiles finally proved it, using mathematics that did not exist in the margin-writer's lifetime.

why: He invented both logarithms and a set of numbered rods for multiplying.
mean: A set of numbered rods used for multiplication by hand
story: A Scottish laird who also invented logarithms cut multiplication tables onto strips of ivory. Line the rods up beside a number and the products can simply be read off and added. It was the pocket calculator of the seventeenth century.

why: He identified the tick-borne bacteria and died of the fever he was studying.
mean: A genus of tiny bacteria carried by ticks, lice and fleas
story: An American pathologist traced spotted fever to ticks, then went to Mexico to study typhus. He caught it from the lice he was working with and died at thirty-nine. The genus was named for him a few years later.

why: He isolated the dysentery bacterium during an epidemic in 1897.
mean: A genus of bacteria causing severe dysentery
story: During a dysentery epidemic that killed a fifth of those infected, a young Japanese bacteriologist isolated the organism from patients' stools and proved it was the cause. He was twenty-six. Both the genus and the toxin it makes carry his name.

why: The genus of pneumonia-causing bacteria was named in his honour.
mean: A genus of bacteria causing pneumonia and other infections
story: A German microbiologist who also spotted the diphtheria organism under his microscope gave his name to a genus of rod-shaped bacteria wrapped in a thick slimy capsule. That capsule is exactly what makes them so hard for the immune system to grip.

why: He identified the plague bacterium in Hong Kong in 1894.
mean: A genus of bacteria including the cause of plague
story: Two researchers found the plague organism in Hong Kong within days of each other in 1894, and for decades the credit was muddled. The genus now carries the name of the one whose samples were clean, who also worked out that rats and their fleas carried it.

why: He first described the gut bacterium in infants in 1885.
mean: A genus of gut bacteria, one species of which is used in every laboratory
story: A paediatrician studying infant digestion described a rod-shaped bacterium living harmlessly in the gut. It was renamed in his honour after his death, and the species is now the most studied organism on earth after ourselves.

who: a Scottish microbiologist and army surgeon (1855-1931)
why: He identified the organism behind Malta fever in 1887.
mean: A genus of bacteria causing undulant fever, caught from livestock
story: A Scottish army surgeon posted to Malta traced the fever wrecking the garrison to an organism in goats' milk. Stopping the milk ration ended the epidemic almost overnight, and the genus was named after him.

who: a spa town in central France
why: A chef named the chilled leek and potato soup after the region of his childhood.
mean: A chilled soup of leek, potato and cream
story: A French chef working at a New York hotel served the leek and potato soup of his childhood cold instead of hot, on a hot summer day. He named it after the spa town near his home, and a Manhattan invention now sounds thoroughly French.

who: a Greek colony in Cilicia whose settlers spoke poor Attic Greek
why: Athenians mocked the colonists' broken grammar and named the fault after their town.
mean: A grammatical mistake, or a breach of good manners
story: Athenian visitors to a distant Greek colony were appalled by the dialect the settlers had drifted into, and turned the town's name into an insult for any mangled sentence. The word later widened to cover social blunders as well as grammatical ones.

who: a famously winding river in Asia Minor, now the Buyuk Menderes
why: The river's extravagant loops gave English its word for wandering.
mean: To wander in loops without hurrying; a bend in a river
story: One river in Asia Minor looped so extravagantly across its flat valley that Greek writers used its name as a byword for anything that would not go straight. Geographers still use it as the technical term for a river bend.

who: the king of Macedon and father of Alexander (382-336 BC)
why: Demosthenes delivered a famous series of attacking speeches against him.
mean: A bitter denunciation delivered in public
story: An Athenian orator spent years warning his city about the ambitions of a northern king, in speeches so fierce that the king's name became the word for any blistering public attack. Cicero later borrowed the form to go after Mark Antony.

who: the Hebrew prophet of the Book of Lamentations
why: His long laments over Jerusalem's fall gave the name for any prolonged complaint.
mean: A long mournful complaint or denunciation
story: A Hebrew prophet warned his city for forty years that disaster was coming, was thrown into a cistern for saying so, and then watched it happen. The book of laments that followed gave English a word for any lengthy, gloomy tirade.

who: a sorcerer in the Acts of the Apostles
why: He offered money for the power to give the Holy Spirit.
mean: The buying or selling of church office or sacred things
story: A sorcerer watched the apostles lay hands on people and offered them cash for the same power. Peter's refusal was blistering. His name became the church's legal term for buying office, and a serious offence for the next eighteen centuries.

who: the river of the Greek underworld
why: Its dark waters gave the word for gloom that is total.
story: Souls were ferried across one black river to reach the land of the dead, and the gods swore their most binding oaths on its water. Anything gloomy enough to suggest that crossing is described with the river's name.

who: the Roman queen of the gods
why: Her stately imposing figure became the compliment for a tall commanding woman.
mean: Tall, stately and imposing, of a woman
story: The Roman queen of the gods was pictured as tall, broad-browed and unmistakably in charge, never girlish. Painters and novelists borrowed her name as a compliment for a woman built on the same commanding scale.

who: the Athenian grove sacred to Apollo Lykeios where Aristotle taught
why: Aristotle's school met in that grove, so its name came to mean a place of learning.
mean: A hall for public lectures, or a school
story: Aristotle taught in a grove outside Athens sacred to Apollo under one of his titles, walking as he lectured. The grove's name became the word for a lecture hall, and in France it still names the secondary school itself.

who: the fact-obsessed schoolmaster in Dickens's Hard Times
why: He demanded nothing but facts and crushed imagination, so his name means that attitude.
mean: A person interested only in hard facts and figures
story: Dickens opened a novel with a schoolmaster demanding facts, nothing but facts, and a girl punished for defining a horse poetically instead of anatomically. His name is now the English word for anyone who measures everything and understands nothing.

who: the cheerfully insolvent optimist in Dickens's David Copperfield
why: He waited endlessly for something to turn up, so his name means hopeful improvidence.
mean: Hopelessly optimistic about money that never arrives
story: Dickens created a man permanently one letter away from ruin who assured everyone that something would turn up. Economists borrowed his budgeting advice, and his name became the word for waiting for rescue instead of arranging one.

why: He built the first fully automatic machine gun, recoil-operated.
mean: The first recoil-operated automatic machine gun
story: An American inventor in London decided that the surest way to make money in Europe was to help Europeans kill each other more efficiently. He used the recoil of each shot to load the next, and one man could suddenly do the work of a hundred riflemen.

why: He designed the pistols and machine guns that armies bought for a century.
mean: A pistol or machine gun of an American design
story: A gunsmith's son in Utah filed his first patent at twenty-four and ended with a hundred and twenty-eight. He designed the pistol the US Army carried for seventy-four years, and died at his workbench in Belgium with a design half finished.
